The Moduli Space of Heterotic Line Bundle Models:
a Case Study for the Tetra-Quadric

Evgeny I. Buchbinder    Andrei Constantin    Andre Lukas
Abstract

It has recently been realised that polystable, holomorphic sums of line bundles over smooth Calabi-Yau three-folds provide a fertile ground for heterotic model building. Large numbers of phenomenologically promising such models have been constructed for various classes of Calabi-Yau manifolds. In this paper we focus on a case study for the tetra-quadric - a Calabi-Yau hypersurface embedded in a product of four ℂ​ℙ1\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}^{1} spaces. We address the question of finiteness of the class of consistent and physically viable line bundle models constructed on this manifold. Further, for a specific semi-realistic example, we explore the embedding of the line bundle sum into the larger moduli space of non-Abelian bundles, both by means of constructing specific polystable non-Abelian bundles and by turning on VEVs in the associated low-energy theory. In this context, we explore the fate of the Higgs doublets as we move in bundle moduli space. The non-Abelian compactifications thus constructed lead to S​U​(5)SU(5) GUT models with an additional global B−LB-L symmetry. The non-Abelian compactifications inherit many of the appealing phenomenological features of the Abelian model, such as the absence of dimension four and dimension five operators triggering fast proton decay.

1 Introduction

Smooth Calabi-Yau compactifications of the heterotic string and M-theory represent one of the classic and most-developed avenues from string theory to low energy physics [1]. Despite the great interest received over the years, however, this approach, until recently, has led to only a relatively small number of models that satisfy the most basic phenomenologically requirements, such as exhibiting the Standard Model particle content without any exotics [2, 3, 4, 5, 6]. The scarceness of such models, owing to the considerable mathematical complexity involved in the analysis of the compactification geometry, has made it difficult to address more detailed phenomenological questions, such as proton decay or fermion masses, in a meaningful way.

Recently, this situation has changed. In a series of publications [7, 8, 9, 10], a promising class of E8×E8E_{8}\times E_{8} heterotic compactifications, based on line bundle sums, has been proposed and analyzed. These heterotic line bundle models are based on rank four or five Abelian vector bundles over smooth Calabi-Yau three-folds with non-trivial fundamental group. Using line bundle sums, rather than bundles with non-Abelian structure groups, comes with a number of far-reaching advantages. For one, split bundles lead to the presence of additional, normally anomalous U⁡(1)U(1) symmetries which constrain the structure of the low-energy theory and can have interesting phenomenological implications. Further, the split nature of the bundle facilitates an efficient algorithmic search for physical models and large numbers of promising examples can be found in this way. Specifically, in Refs. [7, 8] over 200 S​U​(5)SU(5) GUT models were constructed on discrete quotients of complete intersection Calabi-Yau manifolds. All these have precisely three generations of GUT families, no anti-families, at least one 𝟓−𝟓¯\mathbf{5}-\overline{\mathbf{5}} pair of Higgs fields and no other matter charged under the GUT group. After forming quotients by the freely-acting discrete symmetries and including Wilson lines, these models led to about 2000 models with the MSSM matter field spectrum plus one or more pair of Higgs doublets. In Ref. [9], this preliminary search for standard-like models was extended to an exhaustive scan which led to some 35,00035,000 S​U​(5)SU(5) GUT models over the same class of Calabi-Yau manifolds. Finally, in [10], over 100100 S​U​(5)SU(5) models and about 29,00029,000 S​O​(10)SO(10) GUT models were constructed over 1414 Calabi-Yau hypersurfaces embedded in toric varieties. These large numbers are indicative of the huge potential of the line bundle construction.

The present paper will be studying heterotic line bundle models using a complementary approach. Rather than scanning over classes of Calabi-Yau manifolds and large numbers of bundles, we will be focusing on a specific Calabi-Yau manifold, the tetra-quadric hypersurface in (ℂ​ℙ1)×4\left(\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{\!\times 4}, for an in-depth analysis of some aspects of heterotic line bundle models. In particular, we will use the present case study to elaborate on three, related points. Firstly, it was noticed in [9] that the number of viable models reaches a certain saturation limit after repeatedly increasing the range of integers defining the line bundles. While this observation was made computationally, it is less clear how to prove finiteness of the class of relevant vector bundles – essentially poly-stable line bundle sums with fixed total Chern class. We revisit this question here and present various partial results including a finiteness proof which relies on excluding the regions in Kähler moduli space close to the boundary; in physical terms this essentially corresponds to the supergravity approximation.

The second objective of the paper is to present in detail a line bundle model on the tetra-quadric manifold that has modestly attractive phenomenological properties. The model exhibits a superpotential that leads to a rank two up quark mass matrix and, while a rank one matrix may be preferably at this level, this means a perturbative and generically large top Yukawa coupling is present. The down quark and lepton Yukawa matrices are entirely zero at the perturbative level so, for a realistic model, they would have to be generated non-perturbatively. Further, all dimension four and five operators which can lead to fast proton decay are forbidden. This model serves as a starting point for the subsequent analysis of the bundle moduli space.

Finally, perhaps the most important issue is to understand how a given line bundle model is embedded into the larger moduli space of non-Abelian bundles and we will study this question for the aforementioned model on the tetra-quadric. Methodically, this problem can be approached in two complementary ways. From a fundamental point of view, one can attempt to construct non-Abelian bundles which split to the given line bundle sum at a particular locus in bundle moduli space. On the other hand, in the context of the four-dimensional effective theory, the analogous process can be carried out by giving VEVs to the bundle moduli. For our example model, we will consider both approaches as well as the relation between them. Similar studies have been undertaken in [11, 12, 13]. An important question in this context concerns the fate of the Higgs doublet pair. As a vector-like pair, the Higgs is not automatically protected from acquiring a mass as one moves in moduli space. In fact, for most of the semi-realistic models constructed to date, the Higgs doublets are massless only on a specific sub-locus in moduli space and receive a typically super-heavy mass elsewhere. For the line bundle model, we have – by construction – a massless Higgs pair at the Abelian locus, but this is not guaranteed to remain massless as we move into the non-Abelian part of the moduli space. Clearly, the conditions under which Higgs doublets are part of the low-energy spectrum, in low-energy parlance referred to as the μ\mu-problem, is of vital importance for string model building and we will study this question for our example model.

These seemingly dissimilar questions run along a common thread and illustrate several problems which arise when studying the moduli space of heterotic line bundle models. Coming from afar, we identify – for our tetra-quadric example manifold – a substantial, though finite, number of points in this moduli space representing Abelian bundles which lead to phenomenologically promising low-energy theories. In the second step, Section 5, we focus on one of these points and, in the last part, Section 6, we “zoom out” again, this time in order to explore the space of non-Abelian deformations around the chosen point.

The non-Abelian bundles discussed in Section 6 have structure group S​U​(4)×UX​(1)SU(4)\times U_{X}(1) leading to S​U​(5)SU(5) GUT models with an additional global UX​(1)U_{X}(1) symmetry which can be seen as a remnant of the four U⁡(1)U(1) symmetries present at the Abelian locus. Combined with hypercharge, this UX​(1)U_{X}(1) leads to a B−LB-L symmetry. Furthermore, these models have a number of appealing phenomenological features such as a certain hierarchy of Yukawa couplings and the absence of dimension four and dimension five operators leading to a fast proton decay. In part, these operators are forbidden by the surviving UX​(1)U_{X}(1) symmetry. However, it is well known that operators of the form 10 10 10​𝟓¯{\bf 10}\,{\bf 10}\,{\bf 10}\,\overline{\bf 5} are invariant under the UX​(1)U_{X}(1) symmetry. Yet, in our S​U​(5)×UX​(1)SU(5)\times U_{X}(1) models these operators are absent because of the presence of additional U⁡(1)U(1) symmetries which appear at the Abelian locus. Something similar happens with the Higgs multiplets. By construction we have a massless pair of Higgs doublets at the Abelian locus but, as we will see, the U⁡(1)U(1) symmetries also forbid a μ\mu-term with singlet insertions. This means that the Higgs doublets remain massless as we continue away from the Abelian locus to an S​U​(5)×UX​(1)SU(5)\times U_{X}(1) model. These examples demonstrate the power and the advantage of the present approach: we start with an Abelian model which is easier to construct and analyse, but the symmetries which arise at the Abelian locus lead to some degree of control as to which couplings will or will not appear as we move into the non-Abelian part of the moduli space.

The discussion runs on two, even three, levels. On one hand, we have the high energy theory, described in terms of the compactification data: a Calabi-Yau three-fold supplied with a holomorphic, poly-stable bundle. On the other hand, this geometrical set-up leads to a four-dimensional, low-energy supersymmetric GUT, whose gauge group can further be broken to that of the Standard Model. Frequently, we switch back and forth between the high-energy and the effective GUT. The breaking to the Standard Model is only discussed briefly in Section 5, simply to illustrate the virtues of the chosen line bundle model and will be presented in detail elsewhere.

2 Heterotic line bundle models

We begin by reviewing the construction of smooth heterotic compactifications with Abelian bundles. The line bundle construction has been extensively discussed in Refs. [7, 8] and, below, we summarise its most important features, including the derivation of the GUT spectrum. Knowledge of the GUT spectrum will be crucial for the comparison between Abelian and non-Abelian compactifications in Section 6.

2.1 Construction

In the rest of the paper we will discuss E8×E8E_{8}\times E_{8} heterotic line bundle models leading to S​U​(5)SU(5) GUT models. For this purpose, we choose a Calabi-Yau three-fold, XX, with a freely-acting discrete symmetry Γ\Gamma and a vector bundle V→XV\rightarrow X which is given by the sum of line bundles

V=⨁a=15La.V=\bigoplus_{a=1}^{5}L_{a}\;. (2.1)

In practice, we can choose an integral basis, {Ji}\{J_{i}\} of the second cohomology of XX and characterise line bundles by their first Chern class, that is, write La=𝒪⁡(𝐤a)L_{a}={\cal O}({\bf k}_{a}) if c1​(La)=kai​Jic_{1}(L_{a})=k_{a}^{i}J_{i}. 2.2 The Spectrum

For a bundle structure group S⁡(U​(1)5)⊂S​U​(5)⊂E8S(U(1)^{5})\subset SU(5)\subset E_{8} the low-energy gauge group, given by the commutant of the structure group within E8E_{8}, is S​U​(5)×S⁡(U​(1)5)SU(5)\times S\left(U(1)^{5}\right). The matter multiplets present in the four-dimensional theory can be obtained by decomposing the adjoint 𝟐𝟒𝟖E8{\bf 248}_{E_{8}} of E8E_{8} under the S​U​(5)×S⁡(U​(1)5)SU(5)\times S\left(U(1)^{5}\right) sub-group which leads to

𝟏𝟎a,𝟏𝟎¯𝐚,𝟓¯𝐚,𝐛,𝟓𝐚,𝐛,𝟏𝐚,𝐛,{\bf 10}_{a}\;,\quad\overline{\bf 10}_{a}\;,\hskip 11.49994pt\overline{\bf 5}_{a,b}\;,\hskip 11.49994pt{\bf 5}_{a,b}\;,\hskip 11.49994pt{\bf 1}_{a,b}\;, (2.9)

Here the number indicates the S​U​(5)SU(5) representation and the indices a,b,…=1,…​5a,b,\ldots=1,\dots 5 indicate which of the five U⁡(1)U(1) symmetries the multiplet is charged under. Specifically, the 𝟏𝟎a{\bf 10}_{a} (𝟏𝟎¯𝐚\overline{\bf 10}_{a}) multiplets carry charge +1+1 (−1-1) under the atha^{\rm th} U⁡(1)U(1) symmetry while being uncharged under the others. The 𝟓¯𝐚,𝐛\overline{\bf 5}_{a,b} (𝟓a,b{\bf 5}_{a,b}) multiplets carry charge +1+1 (−1-1) under U⁡(1)U(1) charges aa and bb while the singlets 𝟏a,b{\bf 1}_{a,b} carry charge +1+1 under the atha^{\rm th} and charge −1-1 and the bthb^{\rm th} U⁡(1)U(1). The multiplicity of each of these multiplets can be computed from line bundle cohomology, as summarised in Table 1.

The cohomology of line bundles is usually easier to compute than that of non-Abelian bundles and this constitutes another major technical advantage of line bundle models. The phenomenological requirements on the GUT particle spectrum – essentially the three-family constraint plus having an additional 𝟓−𝟓¯{\bf 5}-\overline{\bf 5} pair to account for the Higgs doublets – are summarized in the last column of Table 1.

In order to arrive at a standard-like model, we need a freely-acting symmetry Γ\Gamma on XX, with order |Γ||\Gamma|, which can be lifted to the bundle VV, that is, the bundle VV needs to have a Γ\Gamma– equivariant structure. Then, performing the quotient by Γ\Gamma and including a Wilson line in the hypercharge direction will break the GUT group to the Standard Model group times S⁡(U​(1)5)S(U(1)^{5}). These additional U⁡(1)U(1) symmetries are usually Green-Schwarz anomalous with super-heavy associated gauge bosons and, therefore, do not constitute a phenomenological problem. Upon quotienting by Γ\Gamma, the number 3​|Γ|3|\Gamma| of 𝟏𝟎⊕𝟓¯{\bf 10}\oplus\overline{\bf 5} families which we have required for our GUT models, automatically become 33 standard model families. From the additional 𝟓¯−𝟓\overline{\bf 5}-{\bf 5} multiplets we should keep one pair of Higgs doublets and ensure that all Higgs triplets are projected out. This can frequently be achieved by a suitable choice of equivariant structure and Wilson line. Then, we have a standard model charged spectrum precisely as in the MSSM plus additional moduli fields – the bundle moduli 𝟏a,b{\bf 1}_{a,b} and gravitational moduli – which are uncharged under the standard model group. Our experience is that many such models can be found relatively easily and in this paper we focus on the examples on the tetra-quadric.

3 Heterotic line bundle models on the tetra-quadric

In this section, we focus on the tetra-quadric manifold, discuss its specific properties and present the scan for phenomenologically interesting models on this manifold.

3.1 The tetra-quadric

A detailed discussion of the tetra-quadric, particularly of its Kähler cone, is provided in Appendix A. Here we summarise the most important points. Tetra-quadric Calabi-Yau hypersurfaces are embedded in a product of four ℂ​ℙ1\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}^{1} spaces, defined as the zero locus of some homogeneous polynomial that is quadratic in the homogeneous coordinates of each ℂ​ℙ1\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}^{1} space. Manifolds in this class have Euler number η=−128\eta=-128 and Hodge numbers h1,1​(X)=4h^{1,1}(X)=4 and h2,1​(X)=68h^{2,1}(X)=68. This information is summarised by the following configuration matrix:

X=ℂ​ℙ1ℂ​ℙ1ℂ​ℙ1ℂ​ℙ1​[]−1284,68X~=~~\begin{matrix}\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}^{1}\\ \mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}^{1}\\ \mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}^{1}\\ \mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}^{1}\end{matrix}\!\left[\begin{matrix}~2\!\!\!\!\\ ~2\!\!\!\!&\\ ~2\!\!\!\!&\\ ~2\!\!\!\!\end{matrix}\right]_{-128}^{4,68}\ (3.1)

At certain loci in the complex structure moduli space, the tetraquadric hypersurface admits free actions of finite groups of orders |Γ|=2,4,8,16|\Gamma|=2,4,8,16. Specifically, these groups are Γ=ℤ2,ℤ2×ℤ2,ℤ4\Gamma=\mathbb{Z}_{2},\,\mathbb{Z}_{2}\times\mathbb{Z}_{2},\,\mathbb{Z}_{4}, ℤ2×ℤ4,ℤ8,ℍ,ℤ4×ℤ4,ℤ4⋊ℤ4,ℤ8×ℤ2,ℤ8⋊ℤ2,ℍ×ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}\times\mathbb{Z}_{4},\,\mathbb{Z}_{8},\,\mathbb{H},\,\mathbb{Z}_{4}\times\mathbb{Z}_{4},\,\mathbb{Z}_{4}\rtimes\mathbb{Z}_{4},\,\mathbb{Z}_{8}\times\mathbb{Z}_{2},\,\mathbb{Z}_{8}\rtimes\mathbb{Z}_{2},\,\mathbb{H}\times\mathbb{Z}_{2}. Being at one or another of these special loci corresponds to different choices of coefficients for the monomials composing the defining polynomial, as discussed in Refs. [14, 15]. In other words, saying that the tetraquadric manifold XX admits free quotients by a finite group Γ\Gamma implies a partial fixing of the complex structure of XX. In due course, when we consider line bundle models on the tetra-quadric, some of the Kähler moduli will also be fixed by virtue of the slope zero conditions (2.7).

The tetra-quadric is “favourable” in the sense that its entire second cohomology is spanned by the Kähler forms J1,…,J4J_{1},\ldots,J_{4} of the four ℂ​ℙ1\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}^{1} factors, restricted to the hypersurface. Its cone of Kähler forms J=∑i=14ti​JiJ=\sum_{i=1}^{4}t^{i}J_{i} is given by

C𝐭={𝐭∈ℝ4|ti≥0, 1≤i≤4}C_{{\bf t}}=\left\{{\bf t}\in\mathbb{R}^{4}\ \left|\ t^{i}\geq 0,\,1\leq i\leq 4\right.\right\} (3.2)

and the triple intersection numbers have the following simple form

di​j​k=∫XJi∧Jj∧Jk={2 if ​i≠j,j≠k0 otherwise .d_{ijk}=\int_{X}J_{i}\wedge J_{j}\wedge J_{k}=\begin{cases}2&\mbox{ if }i\neq j,j\neq k\\ 0&\mbox{ otherwise }\end{cases}\;. (3.3)

This leads to the volume form

κ=12​(t1​t2​t3+t1​t2​t4+t1​t3​t4+t2​t3​t4).\kappa=12\left(t_{1}t_{2}t_{3}+t_{1}t_{2}t_{4}+t_{1}t_{3}t_{4}+t_{2}t_{3}t_{4}\right)\;. (3.4)

The second Chern class of the tangent bundle of the tetra-quadric, in the basis {νi}\{\nu^{i}\} of four-forms dual to JiJ_{i}, is given by

c2​(T​X)=(24,24,24,24).c_{2}(TX)=(24,24,24,24)\;. (3.5)

The Mori cone corresponds to all positive linear combinations of νi\nu^{i}.

3.2 Line bundle models

To construct line bundle models on the tetra-quadric we follow the general discussion in Section 2. A line bundle sum is specified by a 4×54\times 5 integer matrix (kai)(k_{a}^{i}) subject to the constraint (2.2) to ensure the vanishing of the first Chern class of the bundle. In Appendix B we provide a more comprehensive account of topological identities of interest for line bundles on the tetra-quadric manifold. Here we focus on the most important quantities, starting with the second Chern class which, from Eqs. (2.3) and (3.3), is given by

c2​i(V)=−2∑a=15(ka2ka3+ka2ka4+ka3ka4,ka1ka3+ka1ka4+ka3ka4,ka1ka2+ka1ka4+ka2ka4,ka1ka2+ka1ka3+ka2ka3)c_{2i}(V)=-2\sum_{a=1}^{5}(k^{2}_{a}k^{3}_{a}+k^{2}_{a}k^{4}_{a}+k^{3}_{a}k^{4}_{a},k^{1}_{a}k^{3}_{a}+k^{1}_{a}k^{4}_{a}+k^{3}_{a}k^{4}_{a},k^{1}_{a}k^{2}_{a}+k^{1}_{a}k^{4}_{a}+k^{2}_{a}k^{4}_{a},k^{1}_{a}k^{2}_{a}+k^{1}_{a}k^{3}_{a}+k^{2}_{a}k^{3}_{a}) (3.6)

relative to the basis {νi}\{\nu^{i}\}. Then, from Eq. (3.5), the anomaly cancellation condition (2.6) becomes

c2​i​(V)≤24.c_{2i}(V)\leq 24\;. (3.7)

Again, from Eqs. (2.3) and (3.3), the index can be computed as

ind⁡(V)=2​∑a=15(ka1​ka2​ka3+ka1​ka2​ka4+ka1​ka3​ka4+ka2​ka3​ka4).{\rm ind}(V)=2\sum_{a=1}^{5}\left(k^{1}_{a}k^{2}_{a}k^{3}_{a}+k^{1}_{a}k^{2}_{a}k^{4}_{a}+k^{1}_{a}k^{3}_{a}k^{4}_{a}+k^{2}_{a}k^{3}_{a}k^{4}_{a}\right)\;. (3.8)

Defining

(κi)=4​(t2​t3+t2​t4+t3​t4,t1​t3+t1​t4+t3​t4,t1​t1+t1​t4+t2​t4,t1​t2+t1​t3+t2​t3)(\kappa_{i})=4(t_{2}t_{3}+t_{2}t_{4}+t_{3}t_{4},t_{1}t_{3}+t_{1}t_{4}+t_{3}t_{4},t_{1}t_{1}+t_{1}t_{4}+t_{2}t_{4},t_{1}t_{2}+t_{1}t_{3}+t_{2}t_{3}) (3.9)

the slope zero conditions (2.7) translate into

μ⁡(La)=κi​kai=!0.\mu(L_{a})=\kappa_{i}k^{i}_{a}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle!}}{{=}}0\;. (3.10)

These conditions need to be satisfied simultaneously for all a=1,…,5a=1,\ldots,5 somewhere in the interior of the Kähler moduli space, so for moduli values ti>0t^{i}>0. Of course, the vanishing of the first Chern class (2.2) ensures that at most four of these conditions are independent. Indeed, for a non-trivial solution of the Eqs. (3.10) at most three of these condition can be independent, so a necessary condition for having a solution with vanishing slope is that the matrix (kai)(k_{a}^{i}) of line bundle integers satsifies

rank⁡(kai)≤3.{\rm rank}(k_{a}^{i})\leq 3\;. (3.11)

Of the four additional U⁡(1)U(1) symmetries, 4−rank⁡(kai)4-{\rm rank}(k^{i}_{a}) are non-anomalous and, hence, have massless gauge bosons at the line bundle locus. From (3.11) this means there is at least one such non-anomalous U⁡(1)U(1) symmetry present for models on the tetra-quadric. Such a U⁡(1)U(1) symmetry is phenomenologically unwanted and it can be spontaneously broken by giving VEVs to the singlets 𝟏a,b{\bf 1}_{a,b}. This corresponds to moving into the non-Abelian part of the moduli space, something we will explore in detail later on in the paper.

The most basic physical constraints on the spectrum are the ones which can be formulated in terms of the index. Most importantly, we have the three-family constraint ind⁡(V)=!−3​|Γ|{\rm ind}(V)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle!}}{{=}}-3|\Gamma| for the 𝟏𝟎{\bf 10} multiplets which, for S​U​(5)SU(5)-bundles, implies that the three-family constraint ind(∧2V)=−3|Γ|{\rm ind}(\wedge^{2}V)=-3|\Gamma| for the 𝟓¯\overline{\bf 5} multiplets is automatically satisfied. In addition, we require that −3​|Γ|≤ind⁡(La⊗Lb)≤0-3|\Gamma|\leq{\rm ind}(L_{a}\otimes L_{b})\leq 0 for all a<ba<b, where the lower limit is just as to not exceed the three-family bound and the upper limit is to avoid chiral 𝟓a,b{\bf 5}_{a,b} multiplets. At the more sophisticated level of cohomology, we should demand the absence of 𝟏𝟎¯\overline{\bf 10} multiplets, that is, h1(X,V∗)=!0h^{1}(X,V^{{}^{*}})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle!}}{{=}}0 and the presence of at least one 𝟓−𝟓¯{\bf 5}-\overline{\bf 5} pair, that is, h1(X,∧2V∗)>!0h^{1}(X,\wedge^{2}V^{{}^{*}})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle!}}{{>}}0. These constraints can be checked using the results from Appendix C where we present an explicit formula for computing line bundle cohomology on the tetra-quadric manifold.

In Ref. [9] a powerful algorithm for systematically generating all line bundle models (kai)(k_{a}^{i}) with entries in the range |kai|≤kmax|k_{a}^{i}|\leq k_{\rm max} for a given upper bound kmaxk_{\rm max} and selecting the models which satisfy all the above constraints has been outlined. In Ref. [9] this algorithm has been applied to the tetra-quadric, among other manifolds, and physically viable models have been extracted. The results are summarized in Table 2. Altogether, 9494 viable GUT models for the available symmetry orders, |Γ|=2,4,8,16|\Gamma|=2,4,8,16, are found. All these models correspond to consistent, anomaly-free and supersymmetric S​U​(5)×S⁡(U​(1)5)SU(5)\times S(U(1)^{5}) GUT theories which satisfy the three-family constraint, have no 𝟏𝟎¯\overline{\bf 10} anti-families and at least one 𝟓−𝟓¯{\bf 5}-\overline{\bf 5} pair to account for the Higgs doublets. Upon taking the quotient by Γ\Gamma and including a Wilson line, many of these become models with an MSSM spectrum and we will study one specific such example below. The complete dataset of viable line bundle sums can be accessed here [16]. The computational evidence that these models indeed represent the complete set of viable models on the tetra-quadric is presented in Fig. 1, where the number of viable models with |kai|≤kmax|k_{a}^{i}|\leq k_{\rm max} is shown as a function of kmaxk_{\rm max}. For all symmetry orders, the number of models saturates at a value of kmaxk_{\rm max} below 1010 and remains stable from thereon. In the next section, we will present various approaches to prove finiteness analytically.

4 Finiteness of the Class of Line Bundle Models

In this section we would like to discuss the problem of finiteness of poly-stable line bundle sums with fixed total Chern class analytically. Specifically, we would like to consider, for the example of the tetra-quadric manifold, the following claim.
Claim: On a given Calabi-Yau three-fold XX and for a fixed rank nn, the number of line bundle sums

V=⨁a=1nLa,La=𝒪X​(𝐤a),V=\bigoplus_{a=1}^{n}L_{a}\;,\quad L_{a}={\cal O}_{X}({\bf k}_{a})\;, (4.1)

satisfying the following properties is finite:

  • •

    c1​(V)=0c_{1}(V)=0 or, equivalently, ∑a=1n𝐤a=0\sum_{a=1}^{n}{\bf k}_{a}=0.

  • •

    The second Chern classes is constrained by c2​(T​X)−c2​(V)∈c_{2}(TX)-c_{2}(V)\in Mori cone of XX.

  • •

    All line bundles have vanishing slope, μ⁡(La)=0\mu(L_{a})=0, simultaneously somewhere in the interior of the Kähler cone of XX.

  • •

    ind⁡(V)=C{\rm ind}(V)=C, where CC is a constant (here taken to be C=−3​|Γ|C=-3|\Gamma|, where |Γ||\Gamma| is the order of a freely-acting symmetry Γ\Gamma on XX).

The automated scan reported on in Ref. [9] and, for the case of the tetra-quadric, illustrated in Fig. 1 provides convincing evidence for the validity of this claim. In fact, as can be seen from those plots, all viable line bundle sums on the tetra-quadric satisfy |kai|≤10|k_{a}^{i}|\leq 10.

Unfortunately, analysing in a straightforward manner the way in which the various above constraints conspire to produce a finite class is untidy. For the tetra-quadric we carry this out explicitly in Appendix D. In the next sub-section, we will prove the above claim for the tetra-quadric and the special case of rank two line bundle sums (n=2n=2). In Section 4.2 we propose a transparent argument to derive a bound for line bundle sums of arbitrary rank; however, in order to make this argument feasible, we have to restrict the Kähler cone by imposing two constraints motivated from physics. We require that all Kähler moduli tit^{i} satisfy ti>1t^{i}>1, a constraint linked to the validity of the supergravity approximation, and finiteness of the Calabi-Yau volume, linked to the finiteness of low-energy coupling constants.

4.1 A workable example: rank two line bundle sums

Rank two line bundle sums with vanishing first Chern class have the form V=L⊕L∗V=L\oplus L^{{}^{*}}, where L=𝒪X​(𝐤)L={\cal O}_{X}({\bf k}), so they are described by a single integer vector 𝐤{\bf k} with four entries kik^{i}. We would like to show that the above claim is valid for this specific class of line bundle sums on the tetra-quadric. We begin with the slope zero condition which represents the main technical difficulty and recall that it can be written as

μ⁡(L)=κi​ki=!0,\mu(L)=\kappa_{i}\,k^{i}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle!}}{{=}}0\;, (4.2)

where the quantities κi=di​j​k​tj​tk\kappa_{i}=d_{ijk}\,t^{j}\,t^{k} have been explicitly given in Eq. (3.9). Here, the moduli tit^{i} have to be in the (interior of the) Kähler cone, C𝐭C_{\bf t}, defined in Eq. 3.2. In order to avoid having to solve a quadric in tit^{i} we introduce the new coordinates 𝐬∈ℝ4{\bf s}\in\mathbb{R}^{4}, defined by 𝐬=f⁡(𝐭)=(κ1,κ2,κ3,κ4)/4{\bf s}=f({\bf t})=\left(\kappa_{1},\kappa_{2},\kappa_{3},\kappa_{4}\right)/4. It turns out, and it is explicitly shown in Appendix A, that the Kähler cone f⁡(C𝐭)f(C_{\bf t}) in these new variables is a dense subset of the cone

C𝐬={𝐬∈ℝ4|𝐧i⋅𝐬≥0,𝐞i⋅𝐬≥0, 1≤i≤4}.C_{{\bf s}}=\left\{{\bf s}\in\mathbb{R}^{4}\ \left|\ {\bf n}_{i}\cdot{\bf s}\geq 0,\ {\bf e}_{i}\cdot{\bf s}\geq 0,\ 1\leq i\leq 4\right.\right\}\;. (4.3)

with 𝐧i=𝐧−𝐞i{\bf n}_{i}={\bf n}-{\bf e}_{i}, 𝐧=(1,1,1,1)/2{\bf n}=(1,1,1,1)/2 and the standard unit vectors 𝐞i{\bf e}_{i} on ℝ4\mathbb{R}^{4}. It is also useful to introduce the cone Cˇ𝐤\check{C}_{\mathbf{k}}, dual to C𝐬C_{\mathbf{s}} which is given by the standard definition Cˇ𝐤={𝐤∈ℝ4|𝐤⋅𝐬≥0,∀𝐬∈C𝐬}\check{C}_{\mathbf{k}}=\{\,{\mathbf{k}}\in\mathbb{R}^{4}\left|{\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{s}}\geq 0,\forall\mathbf{s}\in C_{\mathbf{s}}\right.\}. A straightforward computation shows that it can also be written as

Cˇ𝐤={𝐤∈ℝ4|𝐤⋅𝐞i​j≥0,∀i<j},\check{C}_{\mathbf{k}}=\{\,{\mathbf{k}}\in\mathbb{R}^{4}\left|{\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{e}}_{ij}\geq 0,\forall i<j\right.\}\;, (4.4)

where 𝐞i​j=𝐞i+𝐞j{\mathbf{e}}_{ij}={\mathbf{e}}_{i}+{\mathbf{e}}_{j}. We can now say that the slope zero condition is satisfied iff the equation 𝐬⋅𝐤=0{\bf s}\cdot{\bf k}=0 has a non-trivial solution in the interior C̊𝐬\mathring{C}_{\mathbf{s}} of the cone C𝐬{C}_{\mathbf{s}} and this, in turn, is equivalent to the condition 𝐤∉Cˇ𝐤∪(−Cˇ𝐤)\mathbf{k}\notin\check{C}_{\mathbf{k}}\cup\left(-\check{C}_{\mathbf{k}}\right). Given the structure of the cone Cˇ𝐤\check{C}_{\mathbf{k}}, this means the slope zero condition can be satisfied somewhere in the interior of the Kähler cone precisely if the vector 𝐤{\bf k} has two components ki,kjk_{i},k_{j} with ki+kj>0k_{i}+k_{j}>0 and two components kl,kmk_{l},k_{m} with kl+km<0k_{l}+k_{m}<0. Thus, up to permutations of the components of 𝐤{\bf k}, the slope zero condition can be satsified iff

k1+k2>0​ and ​k1+k3<0​ or\displaystyle k_{1}+k_{2}>0\text{ and }k_{1}+k_{3}<0\text{ or } (4.5)
k1+k2>0​ and ​k3+k4<0\displaystyle k_{1}+k_{2}>0\text{ and }k_{3}+k_{4}<0

Further, the bound on the second Chern class becomes

c2i​(V)\displaystyle c_{2}^{i}(V) =\displaystyle= 4​(k2​k3+k2​k4+k3​k4,k1​k3+k1​k4+k3​k4,k1​k2+k1​k4+k2​k4,k1​k2+k1​k3+k2​k3)\displaystyle 4(k^{2}k^{3}+k^{2}k^{4}+k^{3}k^{4},k^{1}k^{3}+k^{1}k^{4}+k^{3}k^{4},k^{1}k^{2}+k^{1}k^{4}+k^{2}k^{4},k^{1}k^{2}+k^{1}k^{3}+k^{2}k^{3}) (4.6)
≤!\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle!}}{{\leq}} (24,24,24,24).\displaystyle(24,24,24,24)\;.

It can be shown, for example using Mathematica, that the system of integer inequalities given by Eqs. (4.5) and (4.6) has a finite number of solutions 𝐤=(k1,k2,k3,k4)\mathbf{k}=(k_{1},k_{2},k_{3},k_{4}) which all satisfy −7<ki<7-7<k_{i}<7. We note that, in arriving at this result, we have not even used the constraint on the index of VV.

4.2 A bound rooted in Physics

Let us now present a more general finiteness proof which applies to line bundle sums of any rank on the tetra-quadric (and can indeed be applied to other Calabi-Yau manifolds) which, however, requires two additional, physically motivated assumptions.

First recall that the Kähler moduli space metric [17] for a Calabi-Yau manifold can be written as

Gi​j=12​Vol​(X)∫XJi∧⋆Jj=−3(κi​kκ−2​κi​κj3​κ2)G_{ij}=\frac{1}{2\,\text{Vol}(X)}\int_{X}J_{i}\wedge\star J_{j}=-3\left(\frac{\kappa_{ik}}{\kappa}-\frac{2\kappa_{i}\kappa_{j}}{3\kappa^{2}}\right) (4.7)

where Vol​(X)=κ/6\text{Vol}(X)=\kappa/6 is the Calabi-Yau volume with respect to the Ricci-flat metric, κ=di​j​k​ti​tj​tk\kappa=d_{ijk}\,t^{i}\,t^{j}\,t^{k}, κi=di​j​k​tj​tk\kappa_{i}=d_{ijk}\,t^{j}\,t^{k} and κi​j=di​j​k​tk\kappa_{ij}=d_{ijk}\,t^{k}. The slope zero conditions for a line bundle sum of the form (4.1) can be written as

κi​kai=0.\kappa_{i}k_{a}^{i}=0\;. (4.8)

Now consider the sum

∑a𝐤aTG𝐤a=−3κdi​j​k∑akaikajtk=−6κtich2​i(V)≤6κ|𝐭||ch2​i(V)|≤6κ|𝐭||c2​i(TX)|.\sum_{a}{\bf k}_{a}^{T}G\,{\bf k}_{a}=-\frac{3}{\kappa}d_{ijk}\sum_{a}k_{a}^{i}\,k_{a}^{j}\,t^{k}=-\frac{6}{\kappa}t^{i}\,\text{ch}_{2i}(V)\leq\frac{6}{\kappa}|{\bf t}||\text{ch}_{2i}(V)|\leq\frac{6}{\kappa}|{\bf t}||c_{2i}(TX)|\;. (4.9)

Introducing the modified moduli space metric G~=κ​G/(6​|𝐭|)\widetilde{G}=\kappa\,G/(6|{\bf t}|) this means that

∑a𝐤aT​G~​𝐤a≤|c2​i​(T​X)|.\sum_{a}{\bf k}_{a}^{T}\widetilde{G}\,{\bf k}_{a}\leq|c_{2i}(TX)|\;.\vskip-9.0pt (4.10)

For a fixed Kähler class 𝐭{\bf t} in the interior of the Kähler cone, the moduli space metric GG and indeed G~\widetilde{G} are positive definite and, hence, the inequality (4.10) constrains the available integer vectors 𝐤a{\bf k}_{a} to a finite set. This statement applies to all Calabi-Yau three-folds. However, it has a limitation which is relevant for the physics application we are discussing. In physics, we are not interested in fixing the Kähler class, that is, different line bundle sums can satisfy the slope zero conditions for different loci in Kähler moduli space. In particular, we cannot, by the above argument, exclude a sequence of line bundle sums whose associated slope zero loci approach the boundary of the Kähler cone. In such a situation, the eigenvalues of G~\widetilde{G} are no longer bounded from below and the above finiteness argument breaks down.

One way to resolve this difficulty is to restrict the “allowed” region in Kähler moduli space, that is, in essence, exclude points close to the boundary. Specifically, what we require is that all ti>1t^{i}>1 (assuming the Kähler cone is given by ti≥0t^{i}\geq 0, as is the case for the tetra-quadric) and that Vol​(X)≲Vmax\text{Vol}(X)\lesssim V_{\rm max}, for a maximal volume VmaxV_{\rm max}. We are then asking about the number of line bundle sums satisfying all conditions listed in the above claim plus the additional requirement that the slope zero conditions hold in the so-defined portion of Kähler moduli space. The physical motivations for these two conditions are the validity of the supergravity approximation (which requires the internal space to be larger than one in string units) and the finiteness of the low-energy coupling constants (specifically finiteness of the gauge couplings and Newton’s constant which are related to the volume).

This method can be applied to any Calabi-Yau manifold, for which the eigenvalues of G~\widetilde{G} are bounded from below over the region of Kähler moduli space defined above. Let us denote by λmin\lambda_{\rm min} the minimum eigenvalue assumed by G~\widetilde{G} over the specified portion of Kähler moduli space. Clearly, the value of λmin\lambda_{\rm min} depends on the specific Calabi-Yau manifold and the maximal value, VmaxV_{\rm max}, of the volume. If indeed λmin>0\lambda_{\rm min}>0 then Eq. (4.10) leads to the bound

∑a|𝐤a|2≤|c2​(T​X)|λmin.\sum_{a}|{\bf k}_{a}|^{2}\leq\frac{|c_{2}(TX)|}{\lambda_{\rm min}}\;. (4.11)

Let us carry this out explicitly for the tetra-quadric. In this case, the metric G~\widetilde{G} is explicitly given by

G~i​j=1t12+t22+t32+t42​(∑a<b<cta​tb​tc)−1​∑a,b≠i,ja<bta2​tb2\widetilde{G}_{ij}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{t_{1}^{2}+t_{2}^{2}+t_{3}^{2}+t_{4}^{2}}}\,\left({\displaystyle\sum_{a<b<c}t_{a}\,t_{b}\,t_{c}}\right)^{-1}\,{\displaystyle\sum_{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle a<b}}{{a,b\neq i,j}}}t_{a}^{2}\,t_{b}^{2}} (4.12)

and the bound (4.11) specializes to

∑a|𝐤a|2≤48λmin.\sum_{a}|{\bf k}_{a}|^{2}\leq\frac{48}{\lambda_{\rm min}}\;. (4.13)

The value of 48/λmin48/\lambda_{\text{min}} as a function of VmaxV_{\rm max}, determined by a straightforward numerical scan over the relevant portion of the moduli space, has been plotted in Figure 2. For the explicit models in Table 2 whose slope zero locus intersects the region defined by ti>1t^{i}>1 and Vol⁡(X)≤50{\rm Vol}(X)\leq 50 we find that ∑a|𝐤a|2<50\sum_{a}|{\bf k}_{a}|^{2}<50. Comparing with Fig. 2 this means that, while the bound (4.13) holds, it is actually rather weak and presumably of limited practical use.

5 A line bundle model on the tetra-quadric

In this chapter, we present a specific example taken from the set of phenomenologically viable line bundle models on the tetra-quadric described in the previous section. It is in the context of this model that we will study the question of continuation into the non-Abelian part of the bundle moduli space and the implications for the mass of the Higgs doublets.

5.1 Definition of the model

The bundle VV for the model in question is given by the sum of the following five line bundles

L1=𝒪X​(−1,0,0,1),L2=𝒪X​(−1,−3,2,2),L3=𝒪X​(0,1,−1,0)L4=𝒪X​(1,1,−1,−1),L5=𝒪X​(1,1,0,−2)\begin{array}[]{lllllllllll}L_{1}&=&{\cal O}_{X}(-1,0,0,1)&,&L_{2}&=&{\cal O}_{X}(-1,-3,2,2)&,&L_{3}&=&{\cal O}_{X}(0,1,-1,0)\\ L_{4}&=&{\cal O}_{X}(1,1,-1,-1)&,&L_{5}&=&{\cal O}_{X}(1,1,0,-2)\end{array} (5.1)

so the associated matrix (kai)(k_{a}^{i}) of line bundle integers reads

(kai)=⁡[−1−10110−311102−1−10120−1−2].(k_{a}^{i})=\begin{matrix}\\ \\ \\ \\ \end{matrix}\!\left[\begin{matrix}-1&-1&~~0&~~1&~~1~\\ ~~0&-3&~~1&~~1&~~1~\\ ~~0&~~2&-1&-1&~~0~\\ ~~1&~~2&~~0&-1&-2~\\ \end{matrix}\right]\;. (5.2)

The rows of this matrix sum up to zero, so clearly we have c1​(V)=0c_{1}(V)=0, as required. From Eq. (3.6) we find

c2​i​(V)=(24,8,20,12)c_{2i}(V)=(24,8,20,12) (5.3)

so that the anomaly constraint (3.7) is satisfied. Further, with rank⁡(kai)=3{\rm rank}(k_{a}^{i})=3, the rank constraint is satisfied and all line bundle slopes (3.10) are zero on the ray in Kähler moduli space where κ1=κ2=κ3=κ4\kappa_{1}=\kappa_{2}=\kappa_{3}=\kappa_{4} which corresponds to the diagonal t1=t2=t3=t4t_{1}=t_{2}=t_{3}=t_{4}. Altogether this means we have defined a consistent, supersymmetric GUT model with symmetry S​U​(5)×S⁡(U​(1)5)SU(5)\times S(U(1)^{5}). Since rank⁡(kai)=3{\rm rank}(k_{a}^{i})=3 one linear combination of the U⁡(1)U(1) symmetries is non-anomalous with a massless vector boson at the Abelian locus. This specific linear combination is (0,1,2,0,1)(0,1,2,0,1), the non-trivial vector in the kernel of the matrix (kai)(k_{a}^{i}).

5.2 The GUT spectrum at the Abelian locus

The total dimensions of the relevant cohomology groups (computed, e.g. using the formulae of Appendix C) are given by

h∙(X,V)\displaystyle h^{{}^{\!\bullet}}(X,V) =(0,12,0,0)\displaystyle=\ (0,12,0,0) (5.4)
h∙(X,∧2V)\displaystyle h^{{}^{\!\bullet}}(X,\wedge^{2}V) =(0,15,3,0)\displaystyle=\ (0,15,3,0)
h∙(X,V⊗V∗)\displaystyle h^{{}^{\!\bullet}}(X,V\otimes V^{{}^{*}}) =(5,60,60,5)\displaystyle=\ (5,60,60,5)

Hence, we have a total of 1212 GUT families in 𝟏𝟎⊕𝟓¯{\bf 10}\oplus\overline{\bf 5} plus three 𝟓−𝟓¯{\bf 5}-\overline{\bf 5} pairs and a large number of singlet fields. In order to quotient this GUT model to a three-family standard model we need |Γ|=4|\Gamma|=4 and with Γ=ℤ2×ℤ2\Gamma=\mathbb{Z}_{2}\times\mathbb{Z}_{2} we have such a symmetry available on the tetra-quadric. Before we discuss this in detail we should be more precise on how the GUT spectrum is split up into the various line bundle sectors. For this we compute the following relevant line bundle cohomologies

h∙(X,L2)=(0,8,0,0),h∙(X,L5)=(0,4,0,0)h∙(X,L2⊗L4)=(0,4,0,0),h∙(X,L2⊗L5)=(0,3,3,0)h∙(X,L4⊗L5)=(0,8,0,0),h∙(X,L1⊗L2∗)=(0,0,12,0)h∙(X,L1⊗L5∗)=(0,0,12,0),h∙(X,L2⊗L3∗)=(0,20,0,0)h∙(X,L2⊗L4∗)=(0,12,0,0),h∙(X,L3⊗L5∗)=(0,0,4,0)\begin{array}[]{lllllll}h^{{}^{\!\bullet}}(X,L_{2})&=&(0,8,0,0)&,&h^{{}^{\!\bullet}}(X,L_{5})&=&(0,4,0,0)\\[4.0pt] h^{{}^{\!\bullet}}(X,L_{2}\otimes L_{4})&=&(0,4,0,0)&,&h^{{}^{\!\bullet}}(X,L_{2}\otimes L_{5})&=&(0,3,3,0)\\[4.0pt] h^{{}^{\!\bullet}}(X,L_{4}\otimes L_{5})&=&(0,8,0,0)&,&h^{{}^{\!\bullet}}(X,L_{1}\otimes L_{2}^{*})&=&(0,0,12,0)\\[4.0pt] h^{{}^{\!\bullet}}(X,L_{1}\otimes L_{5}^{*})&=&(0,0,12,0)&,&h^{{}^{\!\bullet}}(X,L_{2}\otimes L_{3}^{*})&=&(0,20,0,0)\\[4.0pt] h^{{}^{\!\bullet}}(X,L_{2}\otimes L_{4}^{*})&=&(0,12,0,0)&,&h^{{}^{\!\bullet}}(X,L_{3}\otimes L_{5}^{*})&=&(0,0,4,0)\end{array}\vskip 12.0pt (5.5)

(5.6)

5.3 The Standard Model spectrum at the Abelian locus

The relevant Γ=ℤ2×ℤ2\Gamma=\mathbb{Z}_{2}\times\mathbb{Z}_{2} symmetry for the above model is the one whose generators are given by the action of the matrices

(100−1),(0110)\left(\begin{array}[]{rr}1&0\\ 0&-1\end{array}\right)\;,\quad\left(\begin{array}[]{rr}0&1\\ 1&0\end{array}\right)\vskip 12.0pt (5.7)

simultaneously on the coordinates of all four ℂ​ℙ1\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}^{1} ambient space factors. For an appropriate choice of equivariant structure and Wilson line, forming the quotient by this symmetry leads to the downstairs spectrum 22 2 Our notation is slightly judicious in that, strictly, we cannot decide at this stage which linear combination of the four available doublets is the down Higgs HH and which ones are the three lepton doublets.

2​ 102, 105,𝟓¯𝟐,𝟒, 2​𝟓¯𝟒,𝟓,𝐇𝟐,𝟓,𝐇¯𝟐,𝟓, 3 1𝟐,𝟏, 3 1𝟓,𝟏, 51𝟐,𝟑, 3 1𝟐,𝟒, 1𝟓,𝟑.2\,{\bf 10}_{2}\,,\;{\bf 10}_{5}\,,\;\overline{\bf 5}_{2,4}\,,\;2\,\overline{\bf 5}_{4,5}\,,\;H_{2,5}\,,\;\overline{H}_{2,5}\,,\;3\,{\bf 1}_{2,1}\,,\;3\,{\bf 1}_{5,1}\,,\;5{\bf 1}_{2,3}\,,\;3\,{\bf 1}_{2,4}\,,\;{\bf 1}_{5,3}\;. (5.8)

Hence, we have precisely three standard model families (which we have listed in GUT notation but should be thought of as being broken up as 𝟏𝟎a→(Qa,ua,ea){\bf 10}_{a}\rightarrow(Q_{a},u_{a},e_{a}) and 𝟓¯𝐚,𝐛→(𝐝𝐚,𝐛,𝐋𝐚,𝐛)\overline{\bf 5}_{a,b}\rightarrow(d_{a,b},L_{a,b}) into standard model multiplets), one pair of Higgs doublets and 1515 bundle moduli singlets. We note that the U⁡(1)U(1) charges are the same for all standard model multiplets originating from the same GUT multiplet and, hence, for the purpose of discussing the implications of S⁡(U​(1)5)S\left(U(1)^{5}\right) invariance, keeping the GUT notation is adequate.

5.4 The superpotential

The superpotential for the fields (5.6) is highly constrained by the S⁡(U​(1)5)S(U(1)^{5}) charges. At the GUT level the only allowed terms, including operators with singlet insertions are

W=λI​J​K​𝟓2,5(I)​𝟏𝟎2(J)​𝟏𝟎5(K)+ρI​J​K​𝟏2,4(I)​𝟓¯𝟒,𝟓(𝐉)​𝟓𝟐,𝟓(𝐊),W=\lambda_{IJK}{\bf 5}_{2,5}^{(I)}{\bf 10}_{2}^{(J)}{\bf 10}_{5}^{(K)}+\rho_{IJK}{\bf 1}_{2,4}^{(I)}\overline{\bf 5}_{4,5}^{(J)}{\bf 5}_{2,5}^{(K)}\;, (5.9)

where the indices I,J,K​…I,J,K\ldots run over various ranges, as indicated by the multiplicities in the GUT spectrum (5.6) and λI​J​K\lambda_{IJK} and ρI​J​K\rho_{IJK} are arbitrary couplings. At the standard model level, the analogous terms for the spectrum (5.8) are

W=λi​H¯2,5​(Q2(i)​u5+Q5​u2(i))+ρα​i​𝟏2,4(α)​L4,5(i)​H¯2,5,W=\lambda_{i}\overline{H}_{2,5}(Q_{2}^{(i)}u_{5}+Q_{5}u_{2}^{(i)})+\rho_{\alpha i}{\bf 1}_{2,4}^{(\alpha)}L_{4,5}^{(i)}\overline{H}_{2,5}\;, (5.10)

where i=1,2i=1,2 labels the two 𝟏𝟎2{\bf 10}_{2} families and the two lepton doublets L4,5L_{4,5} from the two 𝟓¯𝟒,𝟓\overline{\bf 5}_{4,5} multiplets and α=1,2,3\alpha=1,2,3 labels the three singlets 𝟏2,4{\bf 1}_{2,4}.

These results have a number of important implications for the structure of the model and its phenomenology. To discuss this, let us focus on the standard model superpotential (5.10) for concreteness, although analogous statements follow for its GUT counterpart (5.9). The presence of the Yukawa terms means that the up quark mass matrix has rank two and, while a rank one matrix may be preferably at this level, this means a perturbative and generically large top Yukawa coupling is present. The down quark and lepton Yukawa matrices are entirely zero at the perturbative level so, for a realistic model, they would have to be generated non-perturbatively. Further, all operators at dimension four and five which can lead to fast proton decay are forbidden. The point is that, while we certainly do not advertise this model as the one and only standard model from string theory, it does have modestly attractive phenomenological properties and provides a semi-realistic setting for the analysis of the bundle moduli space which we will carry out in the remaining part of the paper.

Specifically, our intention is to explore the moduli space of non-Abelian bundles for which the line bundle sum (5.2) arises as a special locus. From the viewpoint of the four-dimensional effective field theory, the Abelian locus is characterized by the vanishing VEVs of all singlet fields 𝟏a,b{\bf 1}_{a,b}, while switching on such VEVs corresponds to moving away from the Abelian locus into the non-Abelian part of the moduli space. From this point of view, the last term in the superpotential (5.10) for our example model is the most interesting one. At the Abelian locus where, in particular, ⟨𝟏2,4⟩=0\langle{\bf 1}_{2,4}\rangle=0 this term is simply a coupling. However, for ⟨𝟏2,4⟩≠0\langle{\bf 1}_{2,4}\rangle\neq 0 this term will lead to a mass for the Higgs doublets (or rather for the up Higgs and one linear combination of what we have called lepton doublets) and essentially remove the Higgs from the low-energy spectrum. On the other hand, the spectrum (5.8) contains many other singlets which do not appear in the superpotential. A continuation into the non-Abelian part of the moduli space along those singlet directions, while keeping ⟨𝟏2,4⟩=0\langle{\bf 1}_{2,4}\rangle=0, should leave the Higgs doublets massless. Phrased in terms of the GUT theory, the structure of the superpotential (5.9) suggests that three 𝟓−𝟓¯{\bf 5}-\overline{\bf 5} pairs are removed from the low-energy spectrum if ⟨𝟏2,4⟩≠0\langle{\bf 1}_{2,4}\rangle\neq 0 but that these states remain massless in all parts of the non-Abelian moduli space where ⟨𝟏2,4⟩=0\langle{\bf 1}_{2,4}\rangle=0. One goal for the remainder of the paper is to verify these statements from a more fundamental viewpoint, that is, by explicitly constructing families of non-Abelian bundles and computing their cohomology.

6 Non-Abelian deformations

In this section, we would like to discuss two ways of constructing non-Abelian bundles which split into a given line-bundle sum at a specific locus in moduli space and apply these methods to the example presented in the previous section. We will focus on two main bundle constructions, namely extensions and monads.

6.1 Extensions of line bundle sums

Extension bundles provide a method of constructing non-Abelian bundles which split into a given set of line bundles

V=⨁a=1nLa.V=\bigoplus_{a=1}^{n}L_{a}\;. (6.1)

Group the line bundles into two sets, indexed by I⊂{1,…,n}I\subset\{1,\ldots,n\} and I¯={1,…,n}\I\bar{I}=\{1,\ldots,n\}\backslash I, define the sub-bundles VI=⨁a∈ILaV_{I}=\bigoplus_{a\in I}L_{a} and VI¯=⨁a∈I¯LaV_{\bar{I}}=\bigoplus_{a\in\bar{I}}L_{a}, and write down the extension sequence

0⟶VI⟶V~⟶VI¯⟶ 0.0\ \longrightarrow\ V_{I}\ \longrightarrow\ \widetilde{V}\ \longrightarrow\ V_{\bar{I}}\ \longrightarrow\ 0\;. (6.2)

The moduli space of the extension bundles V~\widetilde{V} defined by this short exact sequence is given by

Ext1(VI¯,VI)≅H1(X,VI⊗VI¯∗)=⨁a∈I,b∈I¯H1(X,La⊗Lb∗).{\rm Ext}^{1}(V_{\bar{I}},V_{I})\cong H^{1}(X,V_{I}\otimes V_{\bar{I}}^{{}^{*}})=\bigoplus_{a\in I,b\in{\bar{I}}}H^{1}(X,L_{a}\otimes L_{b}^{{}^{*}})\;. (6.3)

The origin of this space corresponds to the split bundle V~=VI⊕VI¯=V\widetilde{V}=V_{I}\oplus V_{\bar{I}}=V, but away from it V~\widetilde{V} becomes non-Abelian. Note that the tangent space to the bundle moduli space of VV is given by

H1(X,V∗⊗V)=⨁a≠bH1(X,La⊗Lb∗)H^{1}(X,V^{{}^{*}}\!\otimes V)=\bigoplus_{a\neq b}H^{1}(X,L_{a}\otimes L_{b}^{{}^{*}}) (6.4)

and, in general, this is larger than (6.3). However, if H1(X,La⊗Lb∗)≠0H^{1}(X,L_{a}\otimes L_{b}^{{}^{*}})\neq 0 only if a∈Ia\in I and b∈I¯b\in\bar{I} for a suitable choice of II and I¯\bar{I} then the two spaces are indeed the same and the extension sequence captures the full set of non-Abelian deformations. We note that the cohomology H1(X,La⊗Lb∗)H^{1}(X,L_{a}\otimes L_{b}^{{}^{*}}) contains the low-energy singlets earlier denoted 𝟏a,b{\bf 1}_{a,b}. So, if the U⁡(1)U(1) charges {1,…,n}\{1,\ldots,n\} can be split into two disjoint subsets II and I¯\bar{I} such that only singlets 𝟏a,b{\bf 1}_{a,b} with a∈Ia\in I and b∈I¯b\in{\bar{I}} exist then the extension sequence (6.2) is “complete”.

We recall from Eq. (5.6) that the singlet spectrum for our tetra-quadric example consists of 𝟏2,1{\bf 1}_{2,1}, 𝟏5,1{\bf 1}_{5,1}, 𝟏2,3{\bf 1}_{2,3}, 𝟏2,4{\bf 1}_{2,4}, 𝟏5,3{\bf 1}_{5,3}. Hence, for I={2,5}I=\{2,5\} and I¯={1,3,4}\bar{I}=\{1,3,4\} the above completeness condition is indeed satisfied and the relevant extension sequence for our example reads

0⟶VI⟶V~⟶VI¯⟶ 0,VI=L2⊕L5,VI¯=L1⊕L3⊕L40\ \longrightarrow\ V_{I}\ \longrightarrow\ \widetilde{V}\ \longrightarrow V_{\bar{I}}\ \longrightarrow\ 0\;,\quad V_{I}=L_{2}\oplus L_{5}\;,\quad V_{\bar{I}}=L_{1}\oplus L_{3}\oplus L_{4} (6.5)

The line bundles L1,…,L5L_{1},\dots,L_{5} have been defined in Eq. (5.1).

Again, this conforms with the expectation from the four-dimensional effective field theory.

We would now like to explore non-Abelian continuations of line bundle sums using a different method - the monad construction.

6.2 Monads from line bundle sums

Monad bundles provide a relatively straightforward way to construct bundles with non-Abelian structure groups from line bundle sums. On a Calabi-Yau manifold XX, define two line bundle sums

B=⨁α=1rk​(B)𝒪X​(𝐛α),C=⨁μ=1rk​(C)𝒪X​(𝐜μ)B=\bigoplus_{\alpha=1}^{\text{rk}(B)}{\cal O}_{X}({\bf b}_{\alpha})\;,\quad C=\bigoplus_{\mu=1}^{\text{rk}(C)}{\cal O}_{X}({\bf c}_{\mu}) (6.16)

and the bundle V~\widetilde{V} by the short exact sequence

0⟶V~⟶B⟶fC⟶ 00\ \longrightarrow\ \widetilde{V}\longrightarrow\ B\ \stackrel{{\scriptstyle f}}{{\longrightarrow}}\ C\ \longrightarrow\ 0 (6.17)

so that V~≅Ker⁡(f)\widetilde{V}\cong{\rm Ker}(f). Here, f∈Hom(B,C)≅H0(X,C⊗B∗)f\in\text{Hom}(B,C)\cong H^{0}(X,C\otimes B^{{}^{*}}) can be thought off as a rk⁡(C)×rk⁡(B){\rm rk}(C)\times{\rm rk}(B) matrix with entries fμ​α∈H0​(X,𝒪X​(𝐜μ−𝐛α)CLOSEf_{\mu\alpha}\in H^{0}(X,{\cal O}_{X}({\bf c}_{\mu}-{\bf b}_{\alpha}). Of course, it has to be checked that the above sequence is indeed exact for a given choice of map ff which amounts to verifying that Im⁡(f)=C{\rm Im}(f)=C.

6.2.1 Monads with split loci

Typically, a family of monad maps ff, parametrized by the coefficients of the polynomials fa​if_{ai}, is available leading to a family of monad bundles V~\widetilde{V}. Our task is to construct such a family of monad bundles which splits into a given line bundle sum VV at a particular locus in moduli space, that is, for a specific sub-class of maps ff.

An obvious way to proceed would be to define the line bundle sum BB in the monad sequence as B=V⊕B~B=V\oplus\widetilde{B} where VV is the given line bundle sum and B~\widetilde{B} is some other sum of line bundles. If the monad bundle V~\widetilde{V} splits into VV at some locus, it follows that ch⁡(V~)=ch⁡(V){\rm ch}(\widetilde{V})={\rm ch}(V). This necessary property can be built into the construction by choosing the line bundle sum CC in the monad sequence such that ch​(B~)=ch​(C)\text{ch}(\widetilde{B})=\text{ch}(C). The monad map then has a block diagonal structure f=(g,h)f=(g,h), where gg corresponds to the VV-part of BB and hh corresponds to B~\widetilde{B}. At the locus in bundle moduli space where g=0g=0, we have V⊂Ker​(f)V\subset\text{Ker}(f) and this should correspond to the desired split locus. The problem with this construction is that Ker​(f)\text{Ker}(f) may not be a vector bundle when f=(0,h)f=(0,h). Indeed, for the case of the tetra-quadric, the (quadratic) matrix hh degenerates on a co-dimension one locus det​(h)=0\text{det}(h)=0 in the ambient space, which, generically, intersects the tetra-quadric hypersurface.

To avoid this problem we will use the following alternative construction. We start with a monad realisation of the structure sheaf

0⟶𝒪X⟶B~a⟶faC~a⟶ 00\ \longrightarrow\ {\cal O}_{X}\longrightarrow\ \widetilde{B}_{a}\ \stackrel{{\scriptstyle f_{a}}}{{\longrightarrow}}\ \widetilde{C}_{a}\ \longrightarrow\ 0 (6.18)

where B~a\widetilde{B}_{a} and C~a\widetilde{C}_{a} are sums of line bundles satisfying

rk​(B~a)=rk​(C~a)+1andc1​(B~a)=c1​(C~a).\text{rk}(\widetilde{B}_{a})=\text{rk}(\widetilde{C}_{a})+1\ \ \ \text{and}\ \ \ c_{1}(\widetilde{B}_{a})=c_{1}(\widetilde{C}_{a})\;. (6.19)

On the tetra-quadric, apart from the trivial realisation B~a=𝒪X\widetilde{B}_{a}={\cal O}_{X} and C~a=0\widetilde{C}_{a}=0, one can also consider

B~a=𝒪X​(0,0,0,pa)⊕𝒪X​(0,0,0,qa)andC~a=𝒪X​(0,0,0,pa+qa)\widetilde{B}_{a}={\cal O}_{X}(0,0,0,p_{a})\oplus{\cal O}_{X}(0,0,0,q_{a})\ \ \ \text{and}\ \ \ \widetilde{C}_{a}={\cal O}_{X}(0,0,0,p_{a}+q_{a}) (6.20)

where pap_{a} and qaq_{a} are positive integers. For this choice, the map fa=(f1,a,f2,a)f_{a}=(f_{1,a},f_{2,a}) contains two polynomials of multi-degrees (0,0,0,pa)(0,0,0,p_{a}) and (0,0,0,qa)(0,0,0,q_{a}). For generic choices of the polynomials, this map has rank one generically. The rank reduces to zero at points in ℂ​ℙ1\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}^{1} where f1,a=f2,a=0f_{1,a}=f_{2,a}=0 but for sufficiently generic polynomials these equations have no solution in ℂ​ℙ1\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}^{1}. Hence, this indeed provides a monad representation of the structure sheaf. Of course, the integers pap_{a}, qaq_{a} in B~a\widetilde{B}_{a} and C~a\widetilde{C}_{a} can appear in any of the four entries, so that we have a large number of choices on how to represent the structure sheaf as a monad. We can choose the trivial representation or a non-trivial representation characterized by choosing one of the four line bundle components and two integers pap_{a}, qaq_{a}.

Now consider a given line bundle sum V=⨁a=1nLaV=\bigoplus_{a=1}^{n}L_{a}. We can obtain monad representations for the individual line bundles by simply twisting the monad sequence (6.18) with LaL_{a}. This leads to

0⟶La⟶La⊗B~a⟶faLa⊗C~a⟶ 0.0\ \longrightarrow\ L_{a}\longrightarrow\ L_{a}\otimes\widetilde{B}_{a}\ \stackrel{{\scriptstyle f_{a}}}{{\longrightarrow}}\ L_{a}\otimes\widetilde{C}_{a}\ \longrightarrow\ 0\;. (6.21)

For the full line bundle sum VV, we sum these sequences to obtain

0⟶V⟶B⟶fC⟶ 00\ \longrightarrow\ V\longrightarrow\ B\ \stackrel{{\scriptstyle f}}{{\longrightarrow}}\ C\ \longrightarrow\ 0\vskip-21.0pt (6.22)

where

B=⨁a=1nLa⊗B~a,C=⨁a=1nLa⊗C~a,f=diag​(f1,…​fn).B=\bigoplus_{a=1}^{n}L_{a}\otimes\widetilde{B}_{a}\;,\quad C=\bigoplus_{a=1}^{n}L_{a}\otimes\widetilde{C}_{a}\;,\quad f=\text{diag}\left(f_{1},\ldots f_{n}\right)\;. (6.23)

We note that for each line bundle, aa, we can choose B~a\widetilde{B}_{a} and C~a\widetilde{C}_{a} independently, from the range of possibilities explained above, so there is significant flexibility in the construction. For the diagonal form of the monad map ff, as given above, each such choice leads to a monad representation of the original line bundle sum VV. However, the map ff may allow deformations away from this block-diagonal form and then defines a more general class of bundles

0⟶V~⟶B⟶fC⟶ 00\ \longrightarrow\ \widetilde{V}\longrightarrow\ B\ \stackrel{{\scriptstyle f}}{{\longrightarrow}}\ C\ \longrightarrow\ 0 (6.24)

which split into VV at the locus where ff becomes block-diagonal. Since ch⁡(V~)=ch⁡(B)−ch⁡(C)=ch⁡(V){\rm ch}(\tilde{V})={\rm ch}(B)-{\rm ch}(C)={\rm ch}(V) the Chern character of the monad bundle V~\tilde{V} is the same as that of the original line bundle sum VV. Therefore, if c1​(V)c_{1}(V) vanishes and the line bundle sum VV satisfies the anomaly constraint (2.6) then the same is true for the monad bundle V~\tilde{V}.

the map is block-diagonal and V~\widetilde{V} splits into the original line bundle sums VV so the coefficients in those polynomials parametrize the deformations away from the split locus.

It is important to point out that, even though most of our discussion will be carried out on the cover manifold, the line bundle sums BB, CC in Eq. (6.27) are equivariant under the ℤ2×ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}\times\mathbb{Z}_{2} symmetry of the tetra-quadric which we have used for our line bundle model and which has been defined in (5.7). This means that, subject to an appropriate restriction of the monad map ff, the monad bundle V~\widetilde{V} has a ℤ2×ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}\times\mathbb{Z}_{2} equivariant structure and descends to the quotient manifold.

Before we discuss any further properties, it is crucial to check whether the so-defined bundle V~\widetilde{V} is superysmmetric, that is, whether it is poly-stable with slope zero. This is certainly the case at the locus where V~\widetilde{V} splits into the line bundle sum VV (provided the Kähler moduli are chosen along the diagonal t1=t2=t3=t4t_{1}=t_{2}=t_{3}=t_{4} where all line bundle slopes vanish) but away from the split locus this is no longer obvious and has to be checked.

6.2.3 Stability of Monad Bundles

Before we consider the monad bundle V~\widetilde{V}, we would like to review the general definition of poly-stability and outline the algorithm for checking it.

First, we define the slope of a coherent sheaf FF by

μ𝐭​(F)=1rk​(F)​∫Xc1​(F)∧J∧J=di​j​k​c1i​(F)​tj​tk=c1i​(F)​κi\mu_{\bf t}(F)=\frac{1}{\text{rk}(F)}\int_{X}c_{1}(F)\wedge J\wedge J=d_{ijk}\,c_{1}^{i}(F)\,t^{j}\,t^{k}=c_{1}^{i}(F)\,\kappa_{i} (6.30)

Note that this definition depends on the Kähler class J=ti​JiJ=t^{i}J_{i}. A bundle V~\widetilde{V} is said to be stable for a Kähler class 𝐭{\bf t} if μ𝐭​(F)<μ𝐭​(V~)\mu_{\bf t}(F)<\mu_{\bf t}(\widetilde{V}) for all sub-sheafs F⊂V~F\subset\widetilde{V} with 0<rk​(F)<rk​(V~)0<\text{rk}(F)<\text{rk}(\widetilde{V}). Note that, due to the rank restriction on FF, a line bundle is automatically stable. Further, a bundle V~\widetilde{V} is poly-stable if it is a direct sum of stable bundles, V~=U1⊕U2⊕⋯⊕Un\widetilde{V}=U_{1}\oplus U_{2}\oplus\dots\oplus U_{n}, all with the same slope, μ𝐭​(U1)=μ𝐭​(U2)=⋯=μ𝐭​(Un)=μ𝐭​(V~)\mu_{\bf t}(U_{1})=\mu_{\bf t}(U_{2})=\dots=\mu_{\bf t}(U_{n})=\mu_{\bf t}(\widetilde{V}). The bundle V~\widetilde{V} is supersymmetric if it is poly-stable and has slope zero.

Frequently, and indeed for our present example, we are dealing with bundles V~\widetilde{V} with vanishing first Chern class, so that μ𝐭​(V~)=0\mu_{\bf t}(\widetilde{V})=0 automatically. In this case, poly-stability requires that μ𝐭​(Ur)=0\mu_{\bf t}(U_{r})=0, for all r=1,…,nr=1,\ldots,n, and that μ𝐭​(F)<0\mu_{\bf t}(F)<0 for all sub-sheafs F⊂UrF\subset U_{r} with 0<rk⁡(F)<rk⁡(Ur)0<{\rm rk}(F)<{\rm rk}(U_{r}).

For a poly-stable bundle V~\widetilde{V}, its dual V~∗\widetilde{V}^{{}^{*}} and V~⊗L\widetilde{V}\otimes L for any line bundle LL are also poly-stable. A stable bundle V~\widetilde{V} with rk​(V~)>1\text{rk}(\widetilde{V})>1 and vanishing slope must satisfy H0​(X,V~)=H3​(X,V~)=0H^{0}(X,\widetilde{V})=H^{3}(X,\widetilde{V})=0 as well as H0(X,∧kV)=H3(X,∧kV)=0H^{0}(X,\wedge^{k}V)=H^{3}(X,\wedge^{k}V)=0. While the slope of a bundle can be easily computed, finding all coherent sub-sheafs of a given bundle is difficult. A practical algorithm which deals with this complication is as follows. For a sub-sheaf FF of V~\widetilde{V}, define k=rk⁡(F)k={\rm rk}(F) and the line bundle L=∧kFL=\wedge^{k}F. Then LL is a sub-sheaf of ∧kV~\wedge^{k}\widetilde{V} and μ𝐭​(L)=k​μ𝐭​(F)\mu_{\bf t}(L)=k\mu_{\bf t}(F). So the region in the Kähler cone C𝐭C_{\bf t} where the bundle V~\widetilde{V} (with c1​(V~)=0c_{1}(\widetilde{V})=0) is supersymmetric is

CV~={𝐭∈Ct|μ𝐭(L)≤0 for all line bundles L which inject into ∧kV~,k=1,…,rk(V~)−1}.C_{\widetilde{V}}=\{{\bf t}\in C_{\rm t}\,|\,\mu_{\bf t}(L)\leq 0\mbox{ for all line bundles }L\mbox{ which inject into }\wedge^{k}\widetilde{V}\;,k=1,\ldots,{\rm rk}(\widetilde{V})-1\}\;. (6.31)

Note that, while stability requires μ𝐭​(L)<0\mu_{\bf t}(L)<0, we have used μ𝐭​(L)≤0\mu_{\bf t}(L)\leq 0 in the above definition. In fact, at a locus in Kähler moduli space where μ𝐭​(L)=0\mu_{\bf t}(L)=0 the bundle splits into a direct sum and is no longer stable but poly-stable and, hence, still supersymmetric. In Ref. [18] this has been referred to as a stability wall. In the present context, this is of course precisely what we expect to happen when the bundle V~\widetilde{V} splits into a line bundle sum VV. The detailed procedure to find the supersymmetric region based on Eq. (6.31) has been developed in [19, 20] and summarised in Appendix E.

6.2.4 Checking stability for our example

In order to compute the supersymmetric region (6.31) for our bundle V~\widetilde{V} on the tetra-quadric, it is useful to describe the Kähler cone in terms of the variables si=κi=di​j​k​tj​tks_{i}=\kappa_{i}=d_{ijk}\,t^{j}\,t^{k}. We have seen in Eq. (4.3) that, in those variables, the Kähler cone is

C𝐬={𝐬∈ℝ4|𝐬.𝐞i≥0 and 𝐬.𝐧i≥0}.C_{\bf s}=\{\mathbf{s}\in\mathbb{R}^{4}\ |\ \mathbf{s.e}_{i}\geq 0\text{ and }\mathbf{s.n}_{i}\geq 0\}\;. (6.32)

Then, for a line bundle L=𝒪X​(−𝐤)L={\cal O}_{X}(-{\bf k}), the slope is simply given by the dot product μ𝐬(L)=−𝐬⋅𝐤\mu_{\bf s}(L)=-{\bf s}\cdot{\bf k}. The supersymmetric region, expressed in terms of the 𝐬{\bf s} coordinates, can, therefore be written as

CV~={𝐬∈C𝐬|𝐬.𝐤≥0 for any L=𝒪(−𝐤),L injects into ∧kV~,k=1,…,rk(V~)−1}.C_{\widetilde{V}}=\{\mathbf{s}\in C_{\bf s}\,|\,\mathbf{s}.\mathbf{k}\geq 0\text{ for any }L=\mathcal{O}(-\mathbf{k}),\,L\text{ injects into }\wedge^{k}\widetilde{V},\ k=1,\ldots,\text{rk}(\widetilde{V})-1\}\;. (6.33)

Note that this is an intersection of hyperplanes so the supersymmetric region (written in the 𝐬{\bf s} coordinates) forms a cone.

We now need to find all line bundles, LL, on the tetra-quadric which inject into some wedge power of the monad bundle V~\widetilde{V} defined by Eqs. (6.27). Appendix E sets out a number of simple sufficient conditions, based on computing cohomology dimensions only, for line bundles to inject or not to inject. Specifically, these criteria are given in (E.5), (E.11), (E.17), (E.21), (E.22). Carrying out a scan over all line bundles with entries in the range from −3-3 to 33 we collect all line bundles which definitely inject into some power of V~\widetilde{V}, according to our criteria. These line bundles reduce the supersymmetric region to the following:

CV~={𝐬∈C𝐬|𝐬.(1,1,−1,−1)=0 and 𝐬.(−1,1,0,0)≥0 and 𝐬.(1,1,−2,0)≥0}.C_{\widetilde{V}}=\{\mathbf{s}\in C_{\bf s}\,|\,\ \mathbf{s.}(1,1,-1,-1)=0\text{ and }\mathbf{s.}(-1,1,0,0)\geq 0\text{ and }\mathbf{s.}(1,1,-2,0)\geq 0\}\;. (6.34)

Increasing the range of line bundles integers further did not change this region of stability. For some line bundles the simple numerical criteria in Appendix E are not sufficient to decide whether or not they inject. In such cases, we have to compute ranks of relevant maps which is more involved. We will return to this problem in Section 6.2.7 but we note here that, as it turns out, these line bundles do not change the result (6.34).

The first condition in Eq. (6.34) comes from the fact that the line bundle L4=𝒪X​(1,1,−1,−1)L_{4}={\cal O}_{X}(1,1,-1,-1) injects into V~\widetilde{V}, while its dual L4∗L_{4}^{{}^{*}} injects into ∧4V≅V∗\wedge^{4}V\cong V^{{}^{*}}. This means that we are confined to the hyperplace s1+s2=s3+s4s_{1}+s_{2}=s_{3}+s_{4} in Kähler moduli space and that we have a poly-stable split bundle V~=U⊕L4\widetilde{V}=U\oplus L_{4} which corresponds to the locus in bundle moduli space where the entry f(0,0,1,3)f_{(0,0,1,3)} in the monad map (6.28) vanishes. The locus in bundle moduli space where equality holds for all three conditions in (6.34), which corresponds to t1=t2=t3=t4t_{1}=t_{2}=t_{3}=t_{4}, is precisely where the conditions (6.29) have to be satisfied and the bundle fully splits into the line bundle sum (5.1). Note that L4L_{4} is indeed one of the line bundles defining the original line bundle sum (5.1). Therefore, in its supersymmetric moduli space, V~\widetilde{V} does not provide a fully non-Abelian version of this line bundle sum but only “connects” four of the five line bundles. In terms of the effective field theory language, the locus in bundle moduli space where L4L_{4} remains split off corresponds to vanishing VEVs for all 𝟏a,b{\bf 1}_{a,b} which carry a 44–index. From the spectrum (5.6), these are precisely the singlets 𝟏2,4{\bf 1}_{2,4}. Our earlier arguments based on the effective field theory suggested that the three vector-like 𝟓−𝟓¯{\bf 5}-\overline{\bf 5} multiplets (which give rise to the Higgs doublets) remain massless whenever ⟨𝟏2,4⟩=0\langle{\bf 1}_{2,4}\rangle=0 and we have verified this expectation explicitly by computing the cohomology of the extension bundles. Here we see that ⟨𝟏2,4⟩=0\langle{\bf 1}_{2,4}\rangle=0 in the entire supersymmetric moduli space of our monad bundle V~\widetilde{V} so we expect three massless 𝟓−𝟓¯{\bf 5}-\overline{\bf 5} pairs from the cohomology of ∧2V~\wedge^{2}\widetilde{V}. We will now verify this expectation by an explicit compution.

The computation of these cohomology groups proceeds in several stages. In the first step, we need to find the map between the line bundle sums B~⊗C\widetilde{B}\otimes C and S2​CS^{2}C induced by the monad map (6.38). In the second step, we construct the induced map between the various cohomology groups and compute their ranks using the CICY package [21]. A comprehensive exposition on the computation of cohomology groups and of ranks of maps goes beyond the scope of the present paper. The interested reader can find in Ref. [22] an outline of the basic techniques for computing line bundle cohomology on complete intersection Calabi-Yau manifolds in products of projective spaces.

We find that the map H0​(X,B~⊗C)⟶H0​(X,S2​C)H^{0}(X,\widetilde{B}\otimes C)\longrightarrow H^{0}(X,S^{2}C) has rank 9494, while the map between H1​(X,B~⊗C)⟶H1​(X,S2​C)H^{1}(X,\widetilde{B}\otimes C)\longrightarrow H^{1}(X,S^{2}C) has maximal rank 4848. This leads to

h∙(X,Q)=(56,88,0,0)h^{{}^{\!\bullet}}(X,Q)\ \,=\ (56,88,0,0) (6.47)

⊕Ker(H1(X,∧2B~)⟶H1(X,Q))\displaystyle\oplus\text{Ker}\left(H^{1}(X,\wedge^{2}\widetilde{B})\longrightarrow H^{1}(X,Q)\right)

Computing these maps involves several layers of additional complication. To start with, the map H0(X,∧2B~)⟶H0(X,Q)H^{0}(X,\wedge^{2}\widetilde{B})\longrightarrow H^{0}(X,Q) is induced by the bundle map ∧2B~⟶Q\wedge^{2}\widetilde{B}\longrightarrow Q which itself has to be determined from the monad map (6.38). However, since

it follows that H0​(X,Q)H^{0}(X,Q) is a subspace of H0​(X,B~⊗C)H^{0}(X,\widetilde{B}\otimes C) and thus the map H0(X,∧2B~)⟶H0(X,Q)H^{0}(X,\wedge^{2}\widetilde{B})\longrightarrow H^{0}(X,Q) is equivalent with the map H0(X,∧2B~)⟶H0(X,B~⊗C)H^{0}(X,\wedge^{2}\widetilde{B})\longrightarrow H^{0}(X,\widetilde{B}\otimes C), with the single difference that, for the latter, the target space is larger. Computing the rank of H0(X,∧2B~)⟶H0(X,Q)H^{0}(X,\wedge^{2}\widetilde{B})\longrightarrow H^{0}(X,Q), we obtain 53. This leaves us with the following tableaux of dimensions

0⟶∧2U⟶∧2B~⟶Q⟶0053563+K8588C00000\begin{array}[]{ccccccccc}0&\longrightarrow&\wedge^{2}U&\longrightarrow&\wedge^{2}\widetilde{B}&\longrightarrow&Q&\longrightarrow&0\\ \\[-12.0pt] &&0&&53&&56&&\\ &&3+K&&85&&88&&\\ &&C&&0&&0&&\\ &&0&&0&&0&&\\ \end{array} (6.50)

where K=dimKer(H1(X,∧2B~)⟶H1(X,Q))K=\text{dim}\,\text{Ker}\left(H^{1}(X,\wedge^{2}\widetilde{B})\longrightarrow H^{1}(X,Q)\right) and C=dimCoker(H1(X,∧2B~)⟶H1(X,Q))C=\text{dim}\,\text{Coker}\left(H^{1}(X,\wedge^{2}\widetilde{B})\longrightarrow H^{1}(X,Q)\right). h∙(X,∧2V~)=h∙(X,L4⊗U)+h∙(X,∧2U)=(0,15+K,3+K,0)h^{{}^{\!\bullet}}(X,\wedge^{2}\widetilde{V})\ \,=\ h^{{}^{\!\bullet}}(X,L_{4}\otimes U)\ +\ h^{{}^{\!\bullet}}(X,\wedge^{2}U)\ \,=\ (0,15+K,3+K,0) (6.51)

where K≥0K\geq 0. We recall that the corresponding cohomology at the split locus (where V~\widetilde{V} splits into the line bundle sum VV in (5.1)) is given by h∙(X,V)=(0,15,3,0)h^{{}^{\!\bullet}}(X,V)=(0,15,3,0). This means that the three massless, vector-like 𝟓−𝟓¯{\bf 5}-\overline{\bf 5} states present at the split locus remain massless throughout the supersymmetric moduli space of V~\widetilde{V}, as expected from our low-energy arguments. In principle, the above cohomology calculation still allows K>0K>0. However, from the viewpoint of the effective field theory, this is not expected. Indeed, as the move away from the split locus by switching on singlet VEVs we may generate mass terms for vector-like pairs, thereby reducing their number, but we do not expect this number to increase. Thus we conclude that K=0K=0.

In summary, our result guarantees the presence of massless 𝟓−𝟓¯{\bf 5}-\overline{\bf 5} multiplets (resulting in Higgs doublets in the downstairs theory) for non-Abelian deformations of the original line bundle sum VV which are of the form V~=L4⊕U\widetilde{V}=L_{4}\oplus U. This result is in perfect agreement with the expectation from the four-dimensional effective theory and the earlier cohomology computation in the context of extension bundles.

However, there is an expectation for this cohomology from low-energy arguments. As we move away from the Abelian locus, three of the four U⁡(1)U(1) symmetries are broken spontaneously and, as a result, three bundle moduli should acquire a mass. With 6060 bundle moduli at the Abelian locus we, therefore, expect that h1(X,V~⊗V~∗)=57h^{1}(X,\widetilde{V}\otimes\widetilde{V}^{{}^{*}})=57 and, from Eq. (6.54), that h1(X,U⊗U∗)=45h^{1}(X,U\otimes U^{{}^{*}})=45.

As such, a non-trivial vacuum value for these singlets breaks the UX​(1)U_{X}(1) and corresponds to moving away from the S⁡(U⁡(4)×UX​(1))S(U(4)\times U_{X}(1)) locus into the moduli space of generic S​U​(5)SU(5) bundles. These are the moduli 𝟏2,4{\bf 1}_{2,4} in the spectrum (5.6). The remaining singlets from H1(X,U⊗U∗)H^{1}(X,U\otimes U^{{}^{*}}) are uncharged under UX​(1)U_{X}(1).

6.2.6 The UX​(1)U_{X}(1) symmetry and B−LB-L

In the present section we will show that the additional global UX​(1)U_{X}(1) symmetry, combined with UY​(1)U_{Y}(1) hypercharge, leads to the well-known B−LB-L symmetry. For this, we need to compute the UX​(1)U_{X}(1) charges of the various multiplets in the low-energy GUT. We do this by considering the sequence of embeddings S⁡(U⁡(4)×UX​(1))⊂S​U​(5)⊂E8S\left(U(4)\times U_{X}(1)\right)\subset SU(5)\subset E_{8}. The matter multiplets can be obtained by decomposing the adjoint 𝟐𝟒𝟖E8\mathbf{248}_{E_{8}} of E8E_{8} under the S​U​(5)×UX​(1)SU(5)\times U_{X}(1) sub-group. The corresponding branching rule has been discussed in Ref. [8], which we review below.

The UX​(1)U_{X}(1) charges of the GUT multiplets can be represented by vectors 𝐪\mathbf{q}. Due to the determinant condition, two such vectors 𝐪\mathbf{q} and 𝐪~\mathbf{\widetilde{q}} have to be identified if 𝐪−𝐪~=ℤ​𝐧\mathbf{q}-\widetilde{\mathbf{q}}=\mathbb{Z}\mathbf{n}, where 𝐧=(4,1)\mathbf{n}=(4,1). We summarise in Table 3 the resulting spectrum. The actual UX​(1)U_{X}(1) charges can be recovered from this description by multiplying a charge vector 𝐪=(q1,q2)\mathbf{q}=(q_{1},q_{2}) with (−1,4)(-1,4).

Looking at the dimensions of the various cohomology groups, as computed in the previous section, we obtain the following spectrum:

12 10−1,12𝟓¯𝟑,𝟑𝟓¯−𝟐,3 5𝟐,12 1−𝟓,𝐡𝟏(𝐗,𝐔⊗𝐔∗) 1𝟎{12\,\bf{10}}_{-1}\;,\quad 12\,\overline{\bf 5}_{3}\;,\hskip 11.49994pt3\,\overline{\bf 5}_{-2}\;,\hskip 11.49994pt3\,{\bf 5}_{2}\;,\hskip 11.49994pt12\,{\bf 1}_{-5}\;,\hskip 11.49994pth^{1}(X,U\otimes U^{{}^{*}})\,{\bf 1}_{0}\vskip-4.0pt (6.55)

It is well-known, in the context of regular S​O​(10)SO(10) GUTs, that the U⁡(1)U(1) factor in the standard decomposition S​O​(10)→S​U​(5)×U⁡(1)SO(10)\rightarrow SU(5)\times U(1) leads to B−LB-L with S​O​(10)SO(10) multiplets branching as

𝟏𝟔S​O​(10)=𝟏−5+𝟓¯3+𝟏𝟎−1,𝟏𝟎S​O​(10)=𝟓2+𝟓¯−2.{\bf 16}_{SO(10)}={\bf 1}_{-5}+{\bar{\bf 5}}_{3}+{\bf 10}_{-1}\;,\quad{\bf 10}_{SO(10)}={\bf 5}_{2}+{\overline{\bf 5}}_{-2}\,.\vskip-4.0pt (6.56)

The observation is that these U⁡(1)U(1) charges precisely coincide with the above UX​(1)U_{X}(1) charges in our model. Explicitly, B−LB-L is given by the following combination

B−L=−15​X+25​YB-L\ =\ -\frac{1}{5}X\,+\,\frac{2}{5}Y\vskip-4.0pt (6.57)

of UX​(1)U_{X}(1) and hypercharge. The absence of operators leading to fast proton decay in our S​U​(5)×UX​(1)SU(5)\times U_{X}(1) model is in part, but not fully, explained by the presence of the UX​(1)U_{X}(1) symmetry. For example, while dimension four operators of the form 𝟓¯​𝟓¯​ 10\overline{\bf 5}\,\overline{\bf 5}\,{\bf 10} are clearly forbidden, dimension five operators 𝟓¯𝟑​ 10−𝟏​ 10−𝟏​ 10−𝟏\overline{\bf 5}_{3}\,{\bf 10}_{-1}\,{\bf 10}_{-1}\,{\bf 10}_{-1} are allowed by the UX​(1)U_{X}(1) symmetry. However, from Eq. (5.9), these operators are forbidden, even at a general point in moduli space, by the additional U⁡(1)U(1) symmetries which arise at Abelian locus.

Let us finish this section with the following comment. The 1212 singlets in our model, charged under UX​(1)U_{X}(1), can be viewed as right-handed neutrinos in analogy with conventional S​O​(10)SO(10) GUTs. As it happens, their number equals the number of families so that the charged spectrum forms 1212 copies of 𝟏𝟔S​O​(10){\bf 16}_{SO(10)}. This means that the UX​(1)U_{X}(1) is non-anomalous. This should be considered a coincidence in this particular model, as, in general, the number of singlets does not have to equal the number of families.

6.2.7 More on stability

In Section 6.2.4 we have argued that the bundle V~\widetilde{V} is poly-stable in the region

CV~={𝐬∈C𝐬|𝐬.(1,1,−1,−1)=0 and 𝐬.(−1,1,0,0)≥0 and 𝐬.(1,1,−2,0)≥0}.C_{\widetilde{V}}=\{\mathbf{s}\in C_{\bf s}\,|\,\ \mathbf{s.}(1,1,-1,-1)=0\text{ and }\mathbf{s.}(-1,1,0,0)\geq 0\text{ and }\mathbf{s.}(1,1,-2,0)\geq 0\}\;. (6.58)

in Kähler moduli space and that, due to the first condition above, it splits into a poly-stable bundle V~=U⊕L4\widetilde{V}=U\oplus L_{4}. This result was based on computing cohomology dimensions only. However, for a complete stability analysis we need to consider line bundles injecting into all wedge powers ∧kV~\wedge^{k}\widetilde{V}, where k=1,…,4k=1,\ldots,4, by computing ranks of relevant maps. In this sub-section, we take up these computations and show that they do not change the above result for the poly-stable region.

Given that our bundle is already split, this task is somewhat simplified. All we need to consider is the line bundles injecting into powers of the rank four bundle UU, that is, into UU, ∧2U\wedge^{2}U and ∧3U\wedge^{3}U, which is the case for a line bundle LL, precisely when H0(X,∧kU⊗L∗)H^{0}(X,\wedge^{k}U\otimes L^{{}^{*}}) is non-trivial. Starting with UU itself, a line bundle LL injects into it precisely if

H0(X,U⊗L∗)≅Ker(H0(B~⊗L∗)⟶H0(C⊗L∗))H^{0}\left(X,U\otimes L^{{}^{*}}\right)\cong\text{Ker}\left(H^{0}\big(\widetilde{B}\otimes L^{{}^{\!*}}\big)\ \longrightarrow\ H^{0}\big(C\otimes L^{{}^{\!*}}\big)\right) (6.59)

is non-trivial. We have computed this kernel for all the line bundles with entries between −3-3 and 33 and have obtained the following set of injecting line bundles:


However, none of these line bundles de-stabilises the cone CV~C_{\widetilde{V}}. To find the line bundles LL injecting into ∧2U\wedge^{2}U, we need to find the non-trivial cohomology groups

H0(X,∧2U⊗L∗)≅Ker(H0(∧2B~⊗L∗)⟶Ker(H0(B~⊗C⊗L∗)⟶H0(S2C⊗L∗))).H^{0}\left(X,\wedge^{2}U\otimes L^{{}^{*}}\right)\cong\text{Ker}\left(H^{0}\big(\wedge^{2}\widetilde{B}\otimes L^{{}^{\!*}}\big)\!\longrightarrow\text{Ker}\big(H^{0}\big(\widetilde{B}\otimes C\otimes L^{{}^{\!*}}\big)\!\longrightarrow\!H^{0}\big(S^{2}C\otimes L^{{}^{\!*}}\big)\big)\!\right)\;. (6.60)

Although computationally challenging, we have computed the cohomology H0(X,∧2U⊗L∗)H^{0}\left(X,\wedge^{2}U\otimes L^{{}^{*}}\right) for all the line bundles with entries between −1-1 and 11 and we find no injecting line bundles.

Finally, for the line bundles that potentially inject into ∧3U\wedge^{3}U we need to compute cohomology groups of the type H0(X,∧3U⊗L∗)H^{0}\left(X,\wedge^{3}U\otimes L^{{}^{*}}\right). 7 Conclusions and Outlook

In this paper, we have presented an in-depth analysis of various aspects of heterotic line bundle models, in the context of a “case-study” for the tetra-quadric Calabi-Yau hyper-surface in (ℂ​ℙ1)×4(\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}^{1})^{\times 4}. First, we have studied the question of finiteness of the class of heterotic line bundle models; mathematically this corresponds to the question of finiteness of poly-stable line bundles sums with fixed total Chern class. On the tetra-quadric, we have proved this finiteness result for the simple case of rank-two line bundle sums of the form L⊕L∗L\oplus L^{{}^{*}}. For higher rank line bundle sums, we have seen that the complication arises at the boundary of Kähler moduli space. Indeed, restricting to the region in Kähler moduli space away from the boundaries (which corresponds to the supergravity approximation) and demanding a finite Calabi-Yau volume, we can show finiteness relatively easily.

From the 9494 phenomemologically promising models on the tetra-quadric which arise for the available group orders |Γ|=2,4,8,16|\Gamma|=2,4,8,16 of freely-acting symmetries, we have chosen a particular example, exhibiting a symmetry Γ=ℤ2×ℤ2\Gamma=\mathbb{Z}_{2}\times\mathbb{Z}_{2}, and we have used this for a more detailed discussion. At the GUT level, this model has gauge group S​U​(5)×U​(1)4SU(5)\times U(1)^{4} (with three of the U⁡(1)U(1) anomalous) and twelve 𝟏𝟎⊕𝟓¯{\bf 10}\oplus\overline{\bf 5} multiplets which lead to precisely three standard model families in the downstairs theory. There are three 𝟓−𝟓¯{\bf 5}-\overline{\bf 5} pairs which, for appropriate Wilson line choices, lead to one pair of Higgs doublets downstairs. In addition, there are 6060 bundle moduli singlets, which reduce to 1515 downstairs. In summary, downstairs, this model has precisely the MSSM spectrum charged under the standard model group plus a number of standard model singlets.

For this model, we have studied the continuation into the non-Abelian part of the moduli space, using the four-dimensional effective theory as well as two different bundle constructions - extensions bundles and monads. Our particular focus was the fate of the Higgs doublets. We found that the only superpotential μ\mu-term allowed by the U​(1)4U(1)^{4} symmetry is of the form 𝟏2,4​L​H¯{\bf 1}_{2,4}\,L\,\bar{H}, where 𝟏2,4{\bf 1}_{2,4} is one type of bundle moduli singlets. Hence, in the part of bundle moduli space where ⟨𝟏2,4⟩=0\langle{\bf 1}_{2,4}\rangle=0 (which includes the line bundle locus, but also non-Abelian S⁡(U⁡(4)×UX​(1))S\left(U(4)\times U_{X}(1)\right)-bundles) the Higgs doublets should remain massless. We have verified this prediction by explicitly constructing the associated non-Abelian bundles, both through extensions and monads, and computing their cohomologies. Hence, we have found a model where the Higgs doublets remain massless away from the purely Abelian line bundle locus, although not in the whole bundle moduli space. We have shown that the remaining UX​(1)U_{X}(1) gives rise to a B−LB-L symmetry of the model.

The line bundle data base [16] contains some models, defined on more complicated Calabi-Yau manifolds, where all μ\mu-terms are forbidden by the U​(1)4U(1)^{4} symmetry. It would be interesting to explicitly study the non-Abelian continuations of these models. We hope that the results of the present paper will be helpful in this context and, more generally, for the task of finding a realistic standard model from string theory.

Appendix C Line Bundle Cohomology on the Tetraquadric

Let XX denote the tetraquadric hypersurface. If the defining polynomial is sufficiently generic, XX is a smooth Calabi-Yau manifold with h1,1​(X)=4h^{1,1}(X)=4. Moreover, this embedding is favourable, in the sense of [9]. This implies that the second cohomology of XX descends entirely from that of the embedding space. As such, all possible line bundles on XX can be obtained as restrictions to XX of line bundles on 𝒜{\cal A}. Let L=𝒪X​(𝐤)L={\cal O}_{X}({\bf k}) be a line bundle with first Chern class defined by a set of four integers kik^{i} as c1​(L)=ki​Jic_{1}(L)=k^{i}J_{i}. For the ease of notation, we order these line bundle integers such that k1≤k2≤k3≤k4k_{1}\leq k_{2}\leq k_{3}\leq k_{4} in the following discussion.

The ranks of the ambient space cohomology groups can be obtained using Bott’s formula:

and the Künneth formula, which gives the cohomology of line bundles over direct products of projective spaces 𝒜=ℂ​ℙn1×…×ℂ​ℙnm{\cal A}=\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}^{n_{1}}\times\ldots\times\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}^{n_{m}}:
