Appendix D Finiteness: a Different Perspective

In Section 4 we have tried to understand the observation, made in Ref. [9], that the number of consistent and physically viable line bundle models constructed over a certain manifold XX admitting discrete symmetries Γ\Gamma of a fixed order is an increasing and saturating function of the maximal line bundle entry in modulus. This phenomenon could be observed for all the pairs (X,|Γ|)(X,|\Gamma|) studied in Ref. [9]. In this section we will argue that the combined effect of cohomology constraints, poly-stability and the bound on the second Chern class imposed by the anomaly cancellation condition limits the range of allowed line bundle integers.

0=μκ​(La)=κ1​ka1+κ2​ka2+κ3​ka3+κ4​ka4.0=\mu_{\kappa}(L_{a})=\kappa_{1}k_{a}^{1}+\kappa_{2}k_{a}^{2}+\kappa_{3}k_{a}^{3}+\kappa_{4}k_{a}^{4}\;. (D.2)

However, due to the condition c1​(V)=0c_{1}(V)=0, only four of these equations are independent. By successively multiplying the above equation by ka1,…,ka4k_{a}^{1},\ldots,k_{a}^{4}, we obtain

Adding these up and summing over aa, we obtain

0\displaystyle 0 =κ1​(∑a=15(ka1)2+−c21+c22+c23+c242)+κ2​(∑a=15(ka2)2++c21−c22+c23+c242)\displaystyle=\kappa_{1}\left(\sum_{a=1}^{5}\left(k_{a}^{1}\right)^{2}+\frac{-c_{2}^{1}+c_{2}^{2}+c_{2}^{3}+c_{2}^{4}}{2}\right)+\kappa_{2}\left(\sum_{a=1}^{5}\left(k_{a}^{2}\right)^{2}+\frac{+c_{2}^{1}-c_{2}^{2}+c_{2}^{3}+c_{2}^{4}}{2}\right) (D.4)

where c21:=c2​(V).J1=∑a=15ka2​ka3+ka2​ka4+ka3​ka4c_{2}^{1}:=c_{2}(V).J_{1}=\sum_{a=1}^{5}k_{a}^{2}k_{a}^{3}+k_{a}^{2}k_{a}^{4}+k_{a}^{3}k_{a}^{4} and analogously for the other indices.

Since κi\kappa_{i} are all positive, and c2ic_{2}^{i} are bounded from above by the anomaly cancellation condition (3.7), it follows that ∑a(ka1)2\sum_{a}\left(k_{a}^{1}\right)^{2}, ∑a(ka2)2\sum_{a}\left(k_{a}^{2}\right)^{2}, ∑a(ka3)2\sum_{a}\left(k_{a}^{3}\right)^{2} and ∑a(ka4)2\sum_{a}\left(k_{a}^{4}\right)^{2} cannot be large at the same time. That is, at least one of the rows in the matrix representing the sum of line bundles has to contain only small numbers.

More significantly, in order to satisfy the above equation with large line bundle entries, some (but not all) of the κi\kappa_{i} parameters have to become small. This corresponds to having some, but not all of the Kähler parameters tit^{i} arbitrarily small. Though not directly relevant for the present discussion, we mention that such a situation falls out of the supergravity approximation, valid when all the Kähler parameters satisfy ti≫1t^{i}\gg 1.

D.3 Combined bounds

The physical constraints on the cohomologies of VV limit the range of line bundle integers in almost all cases. However, these constraints leave three types of line bundles with large integers in modulus, having trivial cohomology. Up to permutations, these are:

  • -

    line bundles with one large integer: 𝒪X​(−1,0,1,±p){\cal O}_{X}(-1,0,1,\pm p)

  • -

    line bundles with two large integers: 𝒪X​(−1,1,±q,±p){\cal O}_{X}(-1,1,\pm q,\pm p)

  • -

    line bundles with four large integers: 𝒪X​(−p,−q,q,p){\cal O}_{X}(-p,-q,q,p)

The third type of line bundles are excluded by stability and the c2​(V)c_{2}(V) constraint discussed above, in Section D.2. Moreover, line bundles of the form 𝒪X​(−1,1,p,q){\cal O}_{X}(-1,1,p,q) where both pp and qq are either positive or negative do not satisfy the slope zero condition in the positive Kähler cone. Thus the only allowed type of line bundles with large entries are of two types:

  • -

    two large integers: 𝒪X​(p,−q,−1,1){\cal O}_{X}(p,-q,-1,1), p,q≥0p,q\geq 0 or

  • -

    𝒪X​(−p,−q,q,p){\cal O}_{X}(-p,-q,q,p) where only p≥0p\geq 0 can be arbitrarily large

We would like to argue that such line bundles, with arbitrarily large entries, cannot enter a viable line bundle model. Before doing that, however, we give an example of an infinite family of line bundle sums satisfying all the topological constraints required from a viable model:

V=⁡[−pp−201100−12−1−1−1−112111−2−1]V~=~~\begin{matrix}\\ \\ \\ \\ \end{matrix}\!\left[\begin{matrix}-p&p-2&~~0&~~1&~~1~\\ ~~0&~~0&-1&~~2&-1~\\ -1&-1&-1&~~1&~~2~\\ ~~1&~~1&~~1&-2&-1~\\ \end{matrix}\right]\; (D.5)

The bundles in this class satisfy, independent of the value of p∈ℤp\in\mathbb{Z}:

c1​(V)\displaystyle c_{1}(V) =0\displaystyle=0 (D.6)
c2​(V).Ji\displaystyle c_{2}(V).J_{i} =(−20,−14,−16,14)\displaystyle=\left(-20,-14,-16,14\right) (D.7)
ind​(V)\displaystyle\text{ind}(V) =ind(∧2V)=12\displaystyle=\text{ind}(\wedge^{2}V)=12 (D.8)

However, the slopes of the above line bundles cannot be simultaneously put to zero in the interior of the Kähler cone, except when p=1p=1.

The following family contains poly-stable line bundle sums for any p∈3​ℤp\in 3\mathbb{Z}:

V=⁡[−pp/3p/3p/300−1−1−13−10001111−2−4]V~=~~\begin{matrix}\\ \\ \\ \\ \end{matrix}\!\left[\begin{matrix}-p&p/3&p/3&p/3&~~0~\\ ~~0&-1&-1&-1&~~3~\\ -1&~~0&~~0&~~0&~~1~\\ ~~1&~~1&~~1&-2&-4~\\ \end{matrix}\right]\; (D.9)

and has

c1​(V)\displaystyle c_{1}(V) =0\displaystyle=0 (D.10)
ind​(V)\displaystyle\text{ind}(V) =ind(∧2V)=24\displaystyle=\text{ind}(\wedge^{2}V)=24 (D.11)

However, the second and the third entries in c2​(V).Jic_{2}(V).J_{i} depend linearly on pp. The two examples above illustrate the conflict between, on one hand, trying to satisfy the slope zero condition and on the other hand trying to keep c2​(V).Jic_{2}(V).J_{i} bounded. If one starts with a line bundle of the type 𝒪X​(−p,−q,q,p){\cal O}_{X}(-p,-q,q,p), one is forced by the slope zero condition to continue with line bundles of the same kind. However, this always leaves at least two entries in c2​(V).Jic_{2}(V).J_{i} large. Alternatively, if one starts with a line bundle 𝒪X​(−p,q,−1,1){\cal O}_{X}(-p,q,-1,1), this will produce at least one large entry in c2​(V).Jic_{2}(V).J_{i}. Trying to make up for that renders the slope zero condition impossible to satisfy.

Appendix E Criteria for Stability of Monad Bundles

If a line bundle LL is a proper sub-bundle of ∧kV\wedge^{k}V, then

HomX(L,∧kV)≅H0(X,∧kV⊗L∗)≠0\text{Hom}_{X}\,\big(L,\wedge^{k}V\big)\cong H^{0}\big(X,\wedge^{k}V\otimes L^{{}^{\!*}}\big)\neq 0 (E.1)

Thus HomX(L,∧k(V))=0\text{Hom}_{X}\big(L,\wedge^{k}(V)\big)=0 guarantees that there are no maps between LL and VV. Below, we derive several criteria for deciding whether HomX(L,∧k(V))\text{Hom}_{X}\big(L,\wedge^{k}(V)\big) is trivial or not. We will use the fact that, for S​U​(n)SU(n) bundles, there exists the isomorphism

∧n−kV≅∧kV∗\wedge^{n-k}V\cong\wedge^{k}V^{{}^{*}} (E.2)

1. The case k=1k=1, L↪VL\hookrightarrow V. By twisting the monad sequence (6.17) with the line bundle L∗L^{{}^{\!*}}, we obtain a short exact sequence which yields the following long exact sequence in cohomology:

0⟶HomX(L,V)⟶H0(B⊗L∗)⟶H0(C⊗L∗)⟶…0\ \longrightarrow\ \text{Hom}_{X}\big(L,V\big)\longrightarrow\ H^{0}\big(B\otimes L^{{}^{\!*}}\big)\ \longrightarrow\ H^{0}\big(C\otimes L^{{}^{\!*}}\big)\ \longrightarrow\ \ldots\vskip-8.0pt (E.3)

Thus

HomX(L,V)≅Ker(H0(B⊗L∗)⟶H0(C⊗L∗))\text{Hom}_{X}\big(L,V\big)\cong\text{Ker}\left(H^{0}\big(B\otimes L^{{}^{\!*}}\big)\ \longrightarrow\ H^{0}\big(C\otimes L^{{}^{\!*}}\big)\right) (E.4)

If h0(B⊗L∗)=0h^{0}\big(B\otimes L^{{}^{\!*}}\big)=0, then LL does not inject into VV. If

h0(B⊗L∗)>h0(C⊗L∗)h^{0}\big(B\otimes L^{{}^{\!*}}\big)>h^{0}\big(C\otimes L^{{}^{\!*}}\big)\vskip-4.0pt (E.5)

then HomX​(L,V)\text{Hom}_{X}\big(L,V\big) is non-trivial. In this case, we will treat LL as a de-stabilising line bundle and restrict the Kähler cone accordingly. In the cases in which these simple cohomology checks are not conclusive, we will need to explicitly find the kernel of the map (E.4).

2. The case k=2k=2, L↪∧2VL\hookrightarrow\wedge^{2}V. Start with the second exterior power sequence:

0⟶∧2V⟶∧2B⟶B⊗C⟶S2C⟶ 00\ \longrightarrow\ \wedge^{2}V\longrightarrow\ \wedge^{2}B\ \longrightarrow\ B\otimes C\ \longrightarrow\ S^{2}C\ \longrightarrow\ 0\vskip-4.0pt (E.6)

then twist this with L∗L^{{}^{\!*}} and split the resulting sequence into two short exact sequences. The associated long exact sequences in cohomology start as:

0⟶HomX(L,∧2V)⟶H0(∧2B⊗L∗)⟶H0(Q)⟶…\displaystyle 0\ \longrightarrow\ \text{Hom}_{X}\big(L,\wedge^{2}V\big)\longrightarrow\ H^{0}\big(\wedge^{2}B\otimes L^{{}^{\!*}}\big)\ \longrightarrow\ H^{0}\big(Q)\ \longrightarrow\ \ldots (E.7)
0⟶H0(Q)⟶H0(B⊗C⊗L∗)⟶H0(S2C⊗L∗)⟶…\displaystyle 0\ \longrightarrow\ H^{0}\big(Q)\ \longrightarrow\ H^{0}\big(B\otimes C\otimes L^{{}^{\!*}}\big)\longrightarrow\ H^{0}\big(S^{2}C\otimes L^{{}^{\!*}}\big)\ \longrightarrow\ \ldots (E.8)

Thus

HomX(L,∧2V)\displaystyle\text{Hom}_{X}\big(L,\wedge^{2}V\big) ≅Ker(H0(∧2B⊗L∗)⟶H0(Q))\displaystyle\cong\text{Ker}\left(H^{0}\big(\wedge^{2}B\otimes L^{{}^{\!*}}\big)\ \longrightarrow\ H^{0}\big(Q\big)\right) (E.9)
H0​(Q)\displaystyle H^{0}(Q) ≅Ker(H0(B⊗C⊗L∗)⟶H0(S2C⊗L∗))\displaystyle\cong\text{Ker}\left(H^{0}\big(B\otimes C\otimes L^{{}^{\!*}}\big)\ \longrightarrow\ H^{0}\big(S^{2}C\otimes L^{{}^{\!*}}\big)\right) (E.10)

As before, there are two simple cohomology checks that can be performed in this case. If h0(∧2B⊗L∗)=0h^{0}\big(\wedge^{2}B\otimes L^{{}^{\!*}}\big)=0, then LL does not inject into ∧2V\wedge^{2}V. However, HomX(L,∧2V)\text{Hom}_{X}\big(L,\wedge^{2}V\big) is non-trivial, if

h0(∧2B⊗L∗)>h0(B⊗C⊗L∗)h^{0}\big(\wedge^{2}B\otimes L^{{}^{\!*}}\big)>h^{0}\big(B\otimes C\otimes L^{{}^{\!*}}\big) (E.11)

3. The case k=3k=3, L↪∧3V≅∧2V∗L\hookrightarrow\wedge^{3}V\cong\wedge^{2}V^{{}^{*}}. There are two relevant sequences in this case. First, start with the dual sequence for ∧2V\wedge^{2}V twisted up with L∗L^{{}^{\!*}}:

0⟶S2C∗⊗L∗⟶B∗⊗C∗⊗L∗⟶∧2B∗⊗L∗⟶∧2V⊗L∗⟶ 00\ \longrightarrow\ S^{2}C^{{}^{*}}\otimes L^{{}^{\!*}}\longrightarrow\ B^{{}^{*}}\otimes C^{{}^{*}}\otimes L^{{}^{\!*}}\ \longrightarrow\ \wedge^{2}B^{{}^{*}}\otimes L^{{}^{\!*}}\ \longrightarrow\ \wedge^{2}V\otimes L^{{}^{\!*}}\ \longrightarrow\ 0\vskip-4.0pt (E.12)

and split this into two short exact sequences with associated long exact sequences in cohomology:

0⟶H0(S2C∗⊗L∗)⟶H0(B∗⊗C∗⊗L∗)⟶H0(Q)⟶H1(S2C∗⊗L∗)⟶…\displaystyle 0\ \longrightarrow\ H^{0}\big(S^{2}C^{{}^{*}}\otimes L^{{}^{\!*}}\big)\longrightarrow\ H^{0}\big(B^{{}^{*}}\otimes C^{{}^{*}}\otimes L^{{}^{\!*}}\big)\ \longrightarrow\ H^{0}\big(Q)\ \longrightarrow\ H^{1}\big(S^{2}C^{{}^{*}}\otimes L^{{}^{\!*}}\big)\longrightarrow\ \ldots
0⟶H0(Q)⟶H0(∧2B∗⊗L∗)⟶HomX(L,∧2V∗)⟶H1(Q)⟶…\displaystyle 0\ \longrightarrow\ H^{0}\big(Q)\ \longrightarrow\ H^{0}\big(\wedge^{2}B^{{}^{*}}\otimes L^{{}^{\!*}}\big)\longrightarrow\ \text{Hom}_{X}\big(L,\wedge^{2}V^{{}^{*}}\big)\ \longrightarrow\ H^{1}\big(Q)\ \longrightarrow\ \ldots\vskip-4.0pt

From here we can infer that HomX(L,∧3V)=0\text{Hom}_{X}\big(L,\wedge^{3}V\big)=0 if h0(∧2B∗⊗L∗)=h1(S2C∗⊗L∗)=h2(S2C∗⊗L∗)=0h^{0}\big(\wedge^{2}B^{{}^{*}}\otimes L^{{}^{\!*}}\big)=h^{1}\big(S^{2}C^{{}^{*}}\otimes L^{{}^{\!*}}\big)=h^{2}\big(S^{2}C^{{}^{*}}\otimes L^{{}^{\!*}}\big)=0.

3’. Alternatively we can start with the third exterior power sequence:

0⟶∧3V⟶∧3B⟶∧2B⊗C⟶B⊗S2C⟶S3C⟶ 00\ \longrightarrow\ \wedge^{3}V\longrightarrow\ \wedge^{3}B\ \longrightarrow\ \wedge^{2}B\otimes C\ \longrightarrow\ B\otimes S^{2}C\ \longrightarrow\ S^{3}C\ \longrightarrow\ 0\vskip-4.0pt (E.13)

then split this sequence into three short exact sequences, whose long exact sequences in cohomology lead to the following indentifications:

HomX(L,∧3V)\displaystyle\text{Hom}_{X}\big(L,\wedge^{3}V\big) ≅Ker(H0(∧3B⊗L∗)⟶H0(Q1))\displaystyle\cong\text{Ker}\left(H^{0}\big(\wedge^{3}B\otimes L^{{}^{\!*}}\big)\ \longrightarrow\ H^{0}\big(Q_{1}\big)\right) (E.14)
H0​(Q1)\displaystyle H^{0}(Q_{1}) ≅Ker(H0(∧2B⊗C⊗L∗)⟶H0(Q2))\displaystyle\cong\text{Ker}\left(H^{0}\big(\wedge^{2}B\otimes C\otimes L^{{}^{\!*}}\big)\ \longrightarrow\ H^{0}\big(Q_{2}\big)\right) (E.15)
H0​(Q2)\displaystyle H^{0}(Q_{2}) ≅Ker(H0(B⊗S2C⊗L∗)⟶H0(S3C⊗L∗))\displaystyle\cong\text{Ker}\left(H^{0}\big(B\otimes S^{2}C\otimes L^{{}^{\!*}}\big)\ \longrightarrow\ H^{0}\big(S^{3}C\otimes L^{{}^{\!*}}\big)\right)\vskip-4.0pt (E.16)

Thus, if h0(∧3B⊗L∗)=0h^{0}\big(\!\wedge^{3}B\otimes L^{{}^{\!*}}\big)=0, then LL does not inject into ∧3V\wedge^{3}V. On the other hand, if

h0(∧3B⊗L∗)>h0(∧2B⊗C⊗L∗)h^{0}\big(\wedge^{3}B\otimes L^{{}^{\!*}}\big)>h^{0}\big(\wedge^{2}B\otimes C\otimes L^{{}^{\!*}}\big)\vskip-4.0pt (E.17)

then HomX(L,∧3V)\text{Hom}_{X}\big(L,\wedge^{3}V\big) is non-trivial.

4. The case k=4k=4, L↪∧4V≅V∗L\hookrightarrow\wedge^{4}V\cong V^{{}^{*}}. In this case, start with the dual monad sequence twisted up with L∗L^{{}^{\!*}}:

0⟶C∗⊗L∗⟶B∗⊗L∗⟶V∗⊗L∗⟶ 00\ \longrightarrow\ C^{{}^{*}}\otimes L^{{}^{\!*}}\longrightarrow\ B^{{}^{*}}\otimes L^{{}^{\!*}}\ \longrightarrow\ V^{{}^{*}}\otimes L^{{}^{\!*}}\ \longrightarrow\ 0\vskip-4.0pt (E.18)

and obtain the long exact sequence in cohomology:

0⟶H0(C∗⊗L∗)⟶H0(B∗⊗L∗)⟶HomX(L,V∗)⟶H1(C∗⊗L∗)⟶…0\ \longrightarrow\ H^{0}\big(C^{{}^{*}}\otimes L^{{}^{\!*}}\big)\longrightarrow\ H^{0}\big(B^{{}^{*}}\otimes L^{{}^{\!*}}\big)\ \longrightarrow\ \text{Hom}_{X}\big(L,V^{{}^{*}})\ \longrightarrow\ H^{1}\big(C^{{}^{*}}\otimes L^{{}^{\!*}}\big)\longrightarrow\ \ldots\vskip-4.0pt (E.19)

This implies the following identification:

HomX(L,V∗)≅Coker(H0(C∗⊗L∗)⟶H0(B∗⊗L∗))⊕Ker(H1(C∗⊗L∗)⟶H1(B∗⊗L∗))\text{Hom}_{X}\big(L,V^{{}^{*}})\cong\text{Coker}\left(H^{0}\big(C^{{}^{*}}\otimes L^{{}^{\!*}}\big)\longrightarrow H^{0}\big(B^{{}^{*}}\otimes L^{{}^{\!*}}\big)\right)\oplus\text{Ker}\left(H^{1}\big(C^{{}^{*}}\otimes L^{{}^{\!*}}\big)\longrightarrow H^{1}\big(B^{{}^{*}}\otimes L^{{}^{\!*}}\big)\right)\vskip 4.0pt (E.20)

If h0(B∗⊗L∗)=h1(C∗⊗L∗)=0h^{0}\big(B^{{}^{*}}\otimes L^{{}^{\!*}}\big)=h^{1}\big(C^{{}^{*}}\otimes L^{{}^{\!*}}\big)=0, then LL does not inject into V∗V^{{}^{*}}. However, HomX(L,V∗)\text{Hom}_{X}\big(L,V^{{}^{*}}) is non-trivial if

h0(C∗⊗L∗)\displaystyle h^{0}\big(C^{{}^{*}}\otimes L^{{}^{\!*}}\big) <h0(B∗⊗L∗) or\displaystyle<h^{0}\big(B^{{}^{*}}\otimes L^{{}^{\!*}}\big)\text{ or } (E.21)
h1(C∗⊗L∗)\displaystyle h^{1}\big(C^{{}^{*}}\otimes L^{{}^{\!*}}\big) >h1(B∗⊗L∗)\displaystyle>h^{1}\big(B^{{}^{*}}\otimes L^{{}^{\!*}}\big)\vskip-4.0pt (E.22)
